House again in Committee of Supply.
Anse aux Gascons-extension of wharf, &c.,

This is to extend the existing wharf to reach 13 feet depth at low water spring tide, to permit the steamers plying on the Baie des Chaleurs, between Gaspe Basin and Dalhousie, to call at all times. This is in Bonaventure county, and the total cost will be $19,000.
Anse aux Gris Fonds-improvements at mouth of river. $2,000.
This is the estimated cost. It is practically to give the fishermen a harbour of refuge.
What county is that in ?

Gasp6.
Anse St. Jean-extension of wharf, $3,000.

This is the total cost of the work, as estimated by the chief engineer. It is to give a depth of from 8 to 16 feet of water at low tide, and it is in Chicoutimi and Saguenay.
Barachoia de Malbaie-breakwater, $5,000.

This is in the county of Gaspe, and the estimated cost of the work is $16,500. It is for the construction of a breakwater.
air. SPROULE. Is this a new work ?

This is the first expenditure on a new work.
air. SPROULE. What is the size of that place ?

It is a very flourishing parish, with a population of 1,300. There is a sand bar there running parallel to the coast line which it is proposed to remove, so as to give boats access to the inner basin. It is a most important fishing - centre, and we have had petitions from the inhabitants praying for this work.
air. HACKETT. Might I ask the kon. minister if he has considered the case of Skinner's Pond in Prince Edward Island ? He is very desirous of promoting the fishing industry, and I can tell him that in the vicinity of Skinner's Pond there is the most important fishing industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that Skinner's Pond item was passed a day or two ago.

I beg to differ. There is no item for Skinner's Pond, and I would like to ask the hon. minister if he will not do something to assist the fishermen there ?
421}

This matter was brought to my attention, and instructions have already been given to the chief engineer of the department to report upon it.
Bonaventure East-breakwater, $5,000.

This is to provide for the construction of a breakwater in Bonaventure county, 700 feet long, 20 feet wide, and to give six feet at low water, spring tide. The total estimated cost of the work is $20,000. It is a new work.
What is the use of a breakwater which will give only six feet of water ?

At the present time a sand bar forms at the mouth of the river, and prevents the fishermen getting into the river, which forms a harbour at that point. The construction of this breakwater will prevent the bar forming, and will give them six feet of water at low spring tide, so that they can take their vessels in.
What is the population of that place V
The population of the township of Bonaventure is 2,682. It is one of the largest parishes on the Baie des Chaleurs.

When we come to an item for a new work, I think the minister should tell us something about the size of the place, its requirements, why the work is needed, and what we are committing the country to in commencing the undertaking. In the province of Ontario a township is about ten miles square, and a harbour or dock usually accommodates two or three townships or more. There is no township in our part of the country with a population of less than 3,000 or 4,000 or 5,000. No one would contend that the fact that a townsip had a population of 2,000 or 3,000 would be any justification for the building of a breakwater. I take it that the people in this township are farmers. There may be a few who fish ; but, so far as I can judge from the information given, this breakwater is for fishing purposes, and not for commercial purposes.

I may say that this township extends wholly along the sea-shore. The townships in the county of Bonaventure are not as they are in Ontario; they are all along the sea-sliore. All these 2,862 people practically will be benefited by this breakwater. It is true, some farming is carried on in the parish, but the main occupation of the people is fishing and lumbering. Probably one hundred fishermen will i>e benefited by this breakwater. The township of St. Bonaventure, by which name it is popularly known, or Hamilton town-

ship, as it is called in the census is one of the largest parishes of the district. At present there is no breakwater or wharf, and the fishermen there have never had any assistance of any kind. They are exposed to storms, especially in the fall, and have no protection whatever for their boats. The steamers that pass there have to land in open boats both people and goods at their inconvenience and sometimes loss. It sometimes happens that steamers pass without being able to stop, and the people have been asking for this improvement for the past thirty years. St. Bonaventure is bound to increase and the time has arrived when something has to be done. In rear of the parish of St. Bonaventure are the famous Robltail'le limits, 40 square miles, given to the family of the late lieutenant governor of the province of Quebec, which are reckoned among the most valuable timber limits in the province. They are still held by the Robitaille family, but in a short time it is expected that they will pass into the hands of a lumber company and be exploited, thus furnishing considerable employment. All are unanimous in the opinion that this work should be done at once.
What is the size of the fishing fleet and to what extent is the industry prosecuted ?

There are about 100 to 125 fishermen in each parish. The importance of the locality was recognized by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he had built at St. Bonaventure the first bait freezing establishment erected in the province of Quebec. The local House passed a special law authorizing the fishermen of the parish to form a bait freezing association at this point.

The hon. member has not told us how many vessels there are in the fishing fleet. Here is a township with a population of 2,862, and we have $10 per head of that population spent at one place. There are 125 fishermen, which would mean $20 per head spent on one small hatchery, and we do not know to what extent the industry is prosecuted and whether there is any commerce carried on there or not. These things may not appear to necessitate a very heavy outlay at the time, but they must be kept up permanently in the future. There ought to be a pretty strong justification before we commence new undertakings of this kind. Here we are proposing to spend about $20,000 to build a breakwater for a harbour, which has not much of a village or town behind it, and only a few fishermen. I am not underestimating the value of the fishermen, because they are a very important class and deserve consideration as well as any other, but if along our shores or lakes- take Georgian bay if you like-in every village where there is a number of fishermen, a breakwater or a wharf is to be built, there will be no end to the expenditure. We Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
are committing ourselves to a dangerous precedent.
This is not an ordinary fishing station. It is a township with a population of 3,000.
They are not all fishermen.

One of the chief industries is the fishing industry. The amount may seem high, but unfortunately the coasts of the Baie des Chaleurs are very shallow' and wharfs have to be built much longer than they otherwise would. If we were to build a $5,000 wharf it would be carried away with the first storm, and the most economical plan is to make a substantial work which will last two or three generations.
How far is that from Gaspe ?
1G0 miles.

I have travelled up that river, the St. Lawrence, and I know that frequently the fishermen of that section labour under great difficulties in getting their products to the market, and any assistance this parliament can give those poor hard working men should be given freely and without comment.
Bois Brfllfi-training pier, &c., $2,000.

This is for a pier 90 feet long and 15 feet wide. It is for the purpose of confining the Witter of the river into one channel in order to give sufficient water for the boats to come in.
Cacouna-extension of wharf, &c., $2,300.
Why do you require to extend it ?

To get into deep water. The extension will be 75 feet and this is to complete.
Caplan-breakwater, $5,000.
Mi'. HACKETT. What county is this in ?

Bonaventure. It is to make provision for the construction of a breakwater 40 feet long and 20 feet wide. The estimated cost is $15,000. It is said in the report that there is no shelter of any kind for the fishing boats. This is also for the purpose of allowing a larger class of boats to engage in the fishing industry at this point. It is also stated in the report that there is at this point an extensive shipping of ties and shingles, and that twenty large vessels, including three barques, loaded there in 1902.
Is the work on the Baie des Chaleurs or ou the gulf ?
On the Baie des Chaleurs.
About what part of it ?
In Bona venture county.
How big is that ?

Perhaps I may be allowed to give a little further explanation with regard to the locality. I may say in answer to the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) that Bonaventure is 150 miles long. GaspC is about 300 miles long.
How much of it is not covered with breakwaters ?

Since confederation, on this Bonaventure coast-line of 150 miles, three small wharfs had been erected ; and out of 19 parishes practically 16 have been left for these 35 years without any protection whatever for the fishermen -no wharfs, no breakwaters, and nothing to facilitate the carrying on of their calling. The parish of St. Charles de Caplan adjoins that of Bonaventure. The census of 1901 shows that this has a population of 1,990. There is this remarkable about Caplan that, in tlie rear a new parish has sprung up, called St. Alphonse de Muselyvilie. This was founded by a Belgian priest, who brought out a Belgian colony and began the first extensive effort to settle the interior of that immense peninsula of 10,000 square miles. This parish of St. Alphonse de Muselyvilie has a population of 900, a resident parish priest, a church and all the facilities and advantages to become a growing and prosperous centre. This population will utilize this new wharf which is to be erected near.the parish church in the middle of the parish coast-line. The fishermen there have now no protection whatever. When they return from fishing they have to get together fifteen or twenty men to haul their boats on the shore, on the approach of the storm, and this work has to be done sometimes in the day-time and sometimes at night. When the steamer passes, people coming ashore have to be lauded on floats. St. Charles de Caplan is a centre and will be the outlet for a considerable trade. The Quebec government last year spent $1,000 in improving the road there, which will make this more a centre than ever. So, I think the expenditure is fully justified. It will have the effect, within the next four or five years, of greatly increasing the business which is done through this point.

I would be glad if the minister would make up a list of the new works he is commencing and the counties in which they are, together with an estimate of the cost of each work when concluded. I presume he has not such a list at hand, but he could probably have it prepared in a short time. We are commencing
many new undertakings on grounds of very doubtful wisdom, if this may be taken as a sample. This work will cost $15,000 or $20,000, and it is to be built at a place where there are only a few fishing boats and about
1.000	people.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will allow me, the parish of St. Charles de Caplan has a population of over 1,900, and in the rear of it is the parish of St. Alphonse de Muselyvilie, with over 800. Both of these parishes will benefit by this wharf. If the amount seems to be large, it is because these wharfs must be built strongly enough to resist the action of the sea. If we were building wharfs on rivers or inland lakes a small expenditure would be sufficient ; but it is no use to erect a wharf at a cost of $4,000 or $5,000 in such a place as this. One storm would carry it away. There was a storm about a month ago at Port Daniel, and the wharf there, a substantial wharf, begun under the late administration, was damaged to the extent of $2,400 in one night.

The outlay would indicate a substantial wharf. I do not object to its being made substantial, because if the work is to be done at ail, it should be done well. But what I complain of is that heavy expenditures are being undertaken, not only for the present, but for the future, upon grounds of questionable wisdom. I can only judge of this by comparing it with my own section of the country. I find important towns, the homes of large fishing fleets and the centres of fine agricultural districts, and with populations three times that mentioned by the hon. gentleman, yet, if it is proposed to spend even $10,000 on a new work, the answer is that the place is too small to justify such a work. Take, for instance, the town of Thornbury, which has a population of 3,000, and has adjacent townships with a population of
15.000	or 20,000. This place is one of the parts of the Georgian bay and the centre of an important commerce. Yet, it would be very difficult to get the government to grant $15,000 to commence a work there. And, even with the most urgent need of commerce and the fishing industry, it is difficult to get the government to grant even $4,000 or $5,000 to keep in proper repair works that may have been built at any of these points. It will be seen that it is not only the amount we are now voting, but the amount necessary to complete the work that must be considered. And. after that, the work must be maintained, so that we are committing ourselves to a never-ending expenditure.

I think the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Sproule's) suggestion is a very proper and reasonable one. 1 thought I had a list such as lie

speaks of, for I desired to have it prepared myself. I do not think that these estimates cover more new works for the province of Quebec than for any other. It is true, as my hon. friend says, that there is no use in spending money on these works at all unless we endeavour to make them substantial. We ought also to understand thoroughly what we are undertaking. With that view I have given the estimates of the chief engineer, which I think are correct as to the total liability to be incurred in each case. My hon. friend will see that out of the ten votes that we have passed for the province of Quebec, only three incur any liability over the amount of the vote, and that the total liability in these cases is only $36,000. I will have a list prepared such as the hon. gentleman desires.
Let me ask the hon. member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil) how it is that the names of the places that he has given in his county do not appear in the last census.

When the county of Bonaventure was originally surveyed it was divided up into townships, and the names of the townships appear in the census. The ecclesiastical authorities have since subdivided these townships into parishes, giving them religious names. For instance, you have St. Bonaventure, representing the township of Hamilton; St. Charles, representing the township of Cap-lan. The member for Dorchester is aware of the system of parishes in Quebec. These divisions are made under the parochial system.

On several occasions, though not recently, I have expressed my opposition to this system of expending public money. I do not wish to take particular exception to this item more than to a large class of similar items that are constantly brought before us. We have necessarily to incur enormous expenditures of a national character. There may come a time when we can, better than now, apply public money to what may be denominated local purposes. I have endeavoured to think this matter- out, and tried to see whether tiie propositions I have heretofore enunciated are fair, that is, whether a work which does not partake of a character which makes it for the general advantage of the Dominion as a whole, is one upon which we are justified in expending federal money. There may be works which cannot be said to affect the whole Dominion, on which the public money of the Dominion can legitimately be applied. But speaking as a rule, and it is a good rule for us to observe, I think that when a work cannot be regarded as a Dominion work distinct from a provincial work, as a Dominion work distinct from a county work or a purely local work, we are not justified in expending

public money upon it. Down by the seashore I have noticed that a good deal of money is spent on harbours, and in procuring facilities for fishermen, and in that instance, when seeing that it will affect more than one province, we can justifiably expend money upon it. It may not be necessary in this case that the money has to be beneficial to more than one province before it can be justifiably spent by the federal parliament. For instance, if you have a public work to be done in some town in the province of Ontario, we might reply to the request of the county council and say: We won't give you a grant for this work. The county council says : It does not affect the county as a whole, therefore we cannot give any public money for it. Now these works, such as the improvement of harbours and small streams, the building of wharfs in places where there is practically no commerce, no interprovincial commerce at all events, are matters of local concern. I know of cases in which the county council would say :	It is a good
local work, it benefits the town where it is being expended, but it does not affect the county as a whole. In these instances I think there should not be a grant of one dollar by the county council, not one dollar by the township council either ; yet they come to this parliament and obtain grants. On what ground ? The only ground upon which they can possibly be justified is that they are a national work in some sense or form. Now I enter my protest against that principle. There may be some qualification of the doctrine, but whilst we have large public enterprises to the fore, whilst we have the necessity for a great expenditure on transportation and other great public works which affect Canada as a whole, whilst we have these and have not sufficient money to satisfy those demands-as we know we have not sufficient money- and when we are going into a large increased expenditure, this year mounting up by the millions, at a rate which is unprecedented, I say that the Minister of Public Works ought not to undertake this long list of new expenditures where it is absolutely certain that these matters cannot be said to be for the general advantage of Canada in any proper sense which would justify us in expending federal money upon them.	.
Now here we have a population, I understand, of some 1,900 in the two parishes. My hon. friend from East Grey has referred to the province of Ontario. I do not care whether it is the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec, neither does my hon. friend, except as an illustration. Take, for instance, the town of Barrie. There was difficulty in getting a grant of $3,000 for a wharf at the town of Barrie. The town of Barrie, now including Allan-dale, has a population of some 6,000, and is rapidly growing. New enterprises are be-

lug launched there this season, and we have difficulty in getting $3,000
On what does the hon. gentleman base his statement that there is difficulty in getting a vote ?

If the hon. gentleman disclaims any effort in that behalf, I withdraw the statement entirely. Probably the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) is perfectly right in suggesting that there was no difficulty in obtaining this vote, inasmuch as, though it was voted several years ago, it has not been implemented by any work done up to the present time. Probably I had better leave the town of Barrie and go a little further down to the new portion of the riding of the hon. member for North Simcoe, where there is a wharf spoken of as the Hawkestone wharf, in the township of Oro. That is another flagrant instance of an expenditure of public money for a purely local purpose. I venture to .say that, except to satisfy a few men in that locality, there is no justification for the expenditure of one dollar of public money upon the Hawkestone wharf. There is no need for it unless it be for a few excursionists who land there from time to time, but very infrequently. This is another instance illustrating the fact that this government is squandering the people's money on wharfs, and what are denominated public works, here and there, for no other purpose, that is self-evident, except to influence the votes of the people in the neighbourhood.	[DOT]
Mr. McCarthy. I do not desire to start an acrimonious discussion but one statement of the hon. gentleman I cannot allow to go unchallenged. His statement about the difficulty of obtaining a grant for the wharf at Barrie of which he spoke is not a correct statement. It has been in the estimates since 1900 ; the difficulty was to decide upon tiie selection of a site. As soon as the situation was agreed upon the work was undertaken. The lumber is now being hauled there aud the work is about to be commenced. In reference to the statement that there was no demand for the Oro wharf, I entirely repudiate that statement on behalf of the township recently added to North Sim-eoe. The hon. gentleman knows very well that his own town of Barrie profits very largely by that wharf. The few excursionists of whom he speaks are farmers who, owing to this cheap transportation come to Barrie more frequently than they otherwise would and sell and buy goods to the advantage of both the townspeople and the farmers.

I deny entirely that a reference to the Hawkestone wharf is in any sense out of order. It is perfectly in order in discussing these estimates to refer to the various works undertaken by the government as illustrations of the fact that we
are not spending money on the works that are properly within the purview of this parliament. When the hon. member says that the. people of Oro are very largely benefited by being able to bring produce to Barrie by the casual boats that call at that wharf from time to time during the excursion season, I can only say that he is not as well informed as perhaps he will be when he becomes more familiar with the people of Oro. There is a railway also passes through the hamlet of Hawkestone and the people who wish to go to market, who do not drive into Barrie, avail themselves of that railway and do not rely upon the fact that once oV twice or three times a week an excursion boat may call at the Hawkestone wharf. In regard to Barrie wharf, I may say that the money has been voted for many years. I am not going to enter into the somewhat difficult question between the hon. member (Mr. McCarthy) and the mayor of Barrie as to the reasons why that money has not been expended. I leave these gentlemen to fight that out among themselves. We have, however, the fact that the money in the first instance was granted just previous to an election, and as it was intended to serve the purpose of another election the work was put off, but a change has come over the spirit of the dream of the hon. member for North Simcoe, who is no longer seeking to represent his native town of Barrie, and so it will no longer serve election purposes as effectively as was expected at the time.
Chambord wharf, $2,000.
Is this a new work, and if so, what is the estimated cost ?

The total cost of this work is estimated at $8,000. It is in the large district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay, and you must recognize that the situation there is somewhat different from that in ordinary parts of the Dominion and of Ontario. The country is settling up and these people have no railway accommodation ; this is the only means they have of getting out their produce ; their only means of transportation is by water. Several of these works are for the purpose of improving the means of transportation in order that the settlers may bring in materials they require and ship out their products.
Is it a village or a fishing station ?
It has a population of 1,020 people along the coast.
Is it the intention of the government to have the works undertaken by public tender and contract ?

All of these new works, these large works, are undertaken by contract.

Chateau Richer-harbour improvements, $4,000.

This item is for harbour improvements at Chateau Richer, which is in the county of Montmorency, Quebec. It is proposed to remove rocks and to improve the passage along the north shore so as to permit barges or batteaux of eight to ten feet to pass safely over the bar and also for the construction of a small crib-work.

I really think it is outrageous to vote $4,000 for that work at Chateau Richer. I know that place thoroughly, and I can say that steamboats never stop there ; boats stop there only when they are forced to do so by a storm. It is a poor place for a boat to land at any time, because a bar extends out into the river for about two miles. The only boats that go there are those which are engaged in the hauling of cord-wood to Quebec. These boats ply between this point and Quebec and they draw four, five or sometimes six feet of water. This is the only purpose for which a wharf is required, and there are two wharfs there already.

Hon. gentlemen sometimes insinuate that these works are assigned to different localities for political purposes. I do not suppose my hon. friend will say that the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) has succeeded in having works given to his constituency as a personal favour. Strong representations have been made to me that this was a very important work. It is represented that most of the inhabitants of Chateau Richer are owners of sailing vessels which are engaged in carrying stone, fire-wood, lime and other materials from points below Quebec to that city, taking back supplies of all kinds from Quebec. It appears that there are there thirty-five boats of a total carrying capacity of 3,500 tons. I am not personally acquainted with the place, but it was on the representations that I brought down this estimate for the purpose of making this improvement. It appeared to me that it was very important in the interests of the population, which numbers between 2,000 and 3,000, and of this very considerable trade which is now going on I should think under the circumstances that this would be a very desirable improvement.

I do not consider politics in dealing with these matters ; I know very well who represents that county in this House, but that makes no difference to me,
I am not speaking from political motives. I do not know any place in the province of Quebec or in Canada that has better railway facilities than Chateau Richer. In summer street cars run through there every ten minutes and in the winter there are three or four trains a day. The settlement is only about twelve miles below Quebec, and I

know well that the only boats which go there go to load stone or cord-wood. You cannot get steamboats to land there because the channel of the river is on the south side right along the Island of Orleans, and when a steamer passes this point it is three or four miles away from Chateau Richer.

Does my hon. friend (Mr. Morin) know that Chateau Richer is an exceedingly important point
because of its impox'tant stone quarries and also as a centre for the distribution of cord-wood. A very large proportion of the cord-wood used in the city of Quebec comes from that locality. In additions to that, as I said, there are very large stone quarries there. I suppose that about 50 per cent of all the stone that is used on macadamized streets in Quebec comes from that locality. It is practically impossible, under existing conditions, for the boats that go there to get into the wharf on account of certain obstacles that exist at that particular point. My hon. friend says that there are good railway facilities there, but I do not think the hon. gentleman would imagine, that they can carry stone or lime or wood on an electric railway. There is no freighting done by the electric railway there, as a matter of fact. As to the steam railway, it is the old story of the competition between water and rail carriage, with the additional disadvantage in this case, that it is a very short haul. It is not twelve miles, but eight miles, to the Montmorency Falls, and Chateau Richer is the second parish below.
How much more than eight miles is it ?

It is nearer twenty miles to this wharf than it is twelve. With respect to the freighting of stone and wood by railway, there would be the additional disadvantage of the high terminal charges at Quebec. Chateau Richer has been a very important centre for a great many years. I have in my own county a place called Beauport at which there is less business done than at Chateau Richer, but the Conservative government built a wharf there, and this government has repaired it although Beauport is within a very few miles of the city of Quebec. If there is any expenditure justifiable in these estimates it is the expenditure for Chateau Richer. It is an important centre which serves a section of the country which is rapidly growing.
I do not rise to prevent this vote passing. If you have a whole lot of money! to waste, go ahead and do it.
Thanks.
Will this complete the work.

It is for the purpose of removing boulders and obstructions at the entrance to the harbour

and in the harbour itself. Of course it is not a great harbour like Quebec ; it is a bay on the north shore of the St. Lawrence and it affords very convenient shipping facilities to the people.

Go ahead ; it is all right.
Desjardins-Allumette wharf, $7,500.

This is a new' work, and the total cost is estimated by the chief engineer at $10,000. There is a small pier there now, and this is for the purpose of giving improved landing and shipping facilities.
Desjardins-Allumette wharf, $7,500.
In what county is this ?

In Pontiac county.
Douglastown-isolated block, $6,000.
What do you mean by nu isolated block ?

This is quite a large and important work and it is in the county of Gaspe. It is to (build an isolated block 450 feet long, 24 feet: wide at the top and from 26 to 30 feet high, giving 12J feet at low water springtide. The total cost of this work will be $30,000. This is the commencement.
Gatineau river-protection of east bank below Canadian Pacific Railway bridge including purchase of land, $3,500.
What is the nature of that work ?

The river was said to be diverted by some government works and an action was brought in the courts, and the Dominion was condemned to pay damages. This is to pay' the balance of the claim and to purchase a certain amount of laud to prevent further claims. It would save a great deal of money if the whole thing had been bought in the first place.
Will this cover the wTliole expense?
This is the whole expense estimated by the government engineer.

Including the cost of the land ?
Grande Riviftre wharf-new covering, $800.
Where is the Grande Riviere?

All right ; go ahead. If it is not in Gaspe county it is pretty sure to be in Bonaventure.
Kamouraska-extension of pier, $4,500.

This is to extend the wharf at Kamouraska,
so as to give a depth of 16 feet at high water.
What boats call at this wharf ?
I am sorry to say I have not the information.

If the minister will allow me, I will tell him. The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Angers) got the government to put on a boat from Malbaie to Kamouraska. That boat is of no use whatever. It only makes a few trips in the summer and none in the winter ; and on the Kamouraska side of the river the govern-men built a wharf only to please a few of their friends.

All I know is that this work was commenced in 1887, and there has been over $23,000 spent upon it. Therefore, I assume that the work is of some importance, and that it will be of great advantage to the local trade, which suffers at present great disadvantages for the want of a sufficient depth of water. This is the total expenditure. There is a petition from the people in favour of the work.
Is there really no definite information as to how often a boat calls ?
I am informed that there is no regular line of boats.
What is the size of the place, and what kind of trade is done ? If only a tramp boat calls there occasionally, it seems to 'be doubtful wisdom to make this expenditure.

Kamouraska is a very important village. In the summer time it is a large watering place. It is the county town of Kamouraska, and up to a few years ago was the judicial seat of the district of Kamouraska, which covered a group of counties. Some years ago the judicial seat was removed to RiviSre du Loup, which is a more growing place. The trade of Kamouraska is chiefly that of a summer resort.
Hear, hear ; we have to pay the expenses of people going in bathing.

No, I did not. I never found fault with any good expenditure.

That is always the answer we get-that the other government did it. The right hon. gentleman got into power because he said we did wrong ; and now, when we criticise anything, he says it was done by us. I can understand that a place might be important enough to have a wharf in days gone by, when there might have been a large local trade in lumber or something of that kind ; but all the conditions may since have changed. The right hon. gentleman tells us that this work is principally for a summer watering place ; and we have to go back to our constituents and tell them that we are voting money from the public exchequer to enable people to go in bathing and to accommodate some boats which carry them food. It is not a work required, for the commerce of the country, because we understand that a steamer calls there only once in a while.
This work amounts to no more to-day than it did before. It was commenced, and it has to be completed or left in an unfinished condition.

The right hon. gentleman's own explanation might be a justification for the commencement of an expenditure years ago which it would not be wise to continue at the present time. He tells us that this place was once a county town and the centre of a judicial district, but that other places having arisen in the meantime, it is not now the county town nor the centre of a judicial centre. There may have been a very important trade done there when the expenditure was commenced, which is now transferred to other places. I notice by the census that the village of Kamouraska has a population of only 578. It may have had a couple of thousand when it was the county town, and there may have been a justification for the expenditure then; but that would be no justification for continuing it if the trade and population have left the place, and the only business now done is by casual excursionists or by people who make a summer resort of the place.

Paspebiac-landing pier, $10,000.

This will be 400 feet long and 30 feet wide, estimated to cost altogether by the engineer $17,000. Paspebiac is the chief shipping port of the county of Bonaventure, in fact of the whole Gaspesian peninsula. There are wharfs now, but they are private property and cannot be used by fishermen and others.
I would ask the minister to state how far Paspebiac is from Quebec.

It is situated on the Baie des Chaleurs. It is the oldest shipping port on the Baie des Chal-eurs, the headquarters of the firm of Clms. Robin, Collas, Cie., one of the largest fishshipping firms in the world, doing business in South America and the West Indies. The aggregate trade at this port last year was $334,000, duty collected, $8,800, as compared with $5,000 two years ago. Strange to say. though Paspebiac has been used as a shipping port for more than 125 years, there has never been a dollar of public money expended at that port. There is a small wharf at present belonging to this shipping firm, from which the fishermen and the general public are excluded. The government has realized the importance of this port, which is open for ten months in the year, and which, at no distant date, I hope will be used by the Intercolonial as a shipping port. The government has thought fit to give this small amount, relatively small compared with the importance of the port. I think the committee will have no objection under the circumstances, in a port of that importance,. to voting this sum for a public wharf there.
I see there is a railway to this place. Is that a branch of the Intercolonial ?

Yes. Unfortunately, the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway belongs to the creditors at present, but it is operated by trustees. It has been extended to Paspebiac, though trains only run to New Carlisle, two miles from Paspebiac ; but there is no doubt that the moment that road gets into the hands either of the Intercolonial or into the hands of a good company, this port of Paspebiac will be utilized. It is one of the most important ports on the whole gulf of the St. Lawrence. Last year I had the honour of producing before this House a statement from Commander Wakeham, of the government steamer ' La Canadienne,' showing that navigation was quite possible for ten months of the year. If the Intercolonial, when it reaches Matapedia, instead of going on through New Brunswick to St. John, or through Nova Scotia to Halifax, simply

branched off down to the Baie des Ohaleurs Railway, and along the shore to Paspebiac, they would have the shortest route from Montreal to Liverpool barring none, not even Sydney, Halifax, St. John, Portland, or any other seaport on the Atlantic.
In this item we have a landing pier costing $10,000 at Paspebiac. What is the meaning of that and what is that pier for ?

To land passengers and freight and to do the general business of the port. There is no landing there now except the company's wharf from which the fishermen are excluded. There are 200 fishermen at this place and they have to land in the mud.

I would ask the minister what revenue he expects to derive from this wharf and any others that we have passed ? The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) has explained the very great amount of business that is done at this port and we might have some estimate as to the probable revenue.

My experience with these fishing stations is that generally the revenue is very small. I could not, with any degree of confidence, give an estimate of the revenue to be derived from this wharf ; I do not expect there would be a very large revenue, judging from our experience with other places.
It is expected that this pier will be used almost altogether by fishing boats and it cannot be expected that very much of this commerce will come to it.

It would be used by the general public as well as by the fishermen. At present there is only one wharf there and it is owned by this firm and is used for the firm's own purposes. The general public is debarred from access to it, except when some special arrangement is made as with the steamer that now performs the mail service.
Does the mail steamer stop there ?
It does.
Does that pay a fee ?
It would pay a fee when it stopped at a public wharf certainly.

It appears to me that this vote is very objectionable. I quite understand that if there were no wharfs at all in this bay the people should be accommodated, but it appears that here that company has built a wharf and that it exacts only such tolls as it has a right to charge the public for the use of the wharf. In our section of the country the wharfs are all
built by private enterprise and of course the owners could not maintain them if they did not charge wharfage. Here is a company that has invested money in the construction of a wharf, and we are told by the hon. gentleman representing that county (Mr. Marcil) that a large sum of money is brought into the country in return for the large exports from that section of the country. Why should we cripple the company that has built a wharf there, if all they want is legitimate fees for the use of that wharf by the public. The government, as I understand, propose to spend $10,000 to build a wharf to cripple the company that has already built a wharf there. If the government constructed a free wharf which would come into competition with the company's wharf it would certainly cripple the company.

I cannot allow the statements of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken to pass uncontradicted. The wharf now in existence at this point is a company's wharf used exclusively for the company's business. There is a population of 1,700 people at Paspebiac who have no wharf accommodation at all. When the House rose 1 was speaking about this vote, and the minister did not give me any information. I am satisfied that no company will refuse wharfage privileges to fishermen or anybody else it' they are willing to pay wharf dues. I don't blame the people for wanting the government to build them a wharf that they can use for nothing, but is it fair to the company who have already spent a large su n of money there in building a wharf. The government will have to borrow this $10,000 at 34 per cent, say, and it will take at least 24 per cent annually to repair this wharf, so that 6 per cent on the $10,000 expenditure would cost us $600 a year. I fancy that if the government wants to go into this business they can make an arrangement with the company to give these fishermen the use of their wharf for less than $600 a year. This expenditure is not justified under the circumstances.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken about the situation there. This is a large company, and they have no more wharf accommodation than is necessary for their own business, so that outside steamers and fishermen cannot use it. I should think that although the receipts from these wharfs are small, as a rule, that in this case they would pay the cost of maintenance. If there was a private wharf there that could be used for public purposes, the case would be different, but my information is that the company use this wharf for their own business, and that it does not afford accommodation for the general trade.

I think the minister must be mistaken about that. Along the shores of Lake Ontario, an incorporated and county towns, where they must have as much business as has Paspebiac, I never heard of a wharf that was not capable of handling all the business that came to it. This company makes its living out of the fishermen, and they are as much interested in accommodating them as in accommodating anybody else. It does not require such a great number of ships to carry away $300,000 worth of fish.

The statistics show that last year 32 vessels entered at that wharf from Great Britain, British West Indies, Brazil, Norway and Sweden, Spain and the United States ; and 60 vessels cleared to Great Britain, British West Indies, Brazil, St. Pierre, Norway and Sweden and the United States. RiviSre Verte-improvements at mouth of, $3,750.
Since the construction of a dam there, there is a flooding each year which damages property.
If this occurs every year, how have we managed in other years when there was no vote ?
This dam causes the ice to jam and then the water overflows. The dredging will prevent that overflow.

The same difficulty arises at the mouth of the Moira river, at Belleville. That city is flooded very often and a large amount of damages caused. Has anything been done to prevent that ? I always understood that the damages were due to the fact that the debris floating down

the river accumulated where the water was shallow and caused it to overflow.

I do not think that that matter has been brought to the attention of the department. My chief engineer says he has no knowledge of it. But of course that being a navigable river, I dare say we would be called upon to do the necessary works to prevent damage.
It is on the bay that the difficulty is where the Moira river flows into it. The accumulation takes place there, not In the river.

We will agree to make the improvements if we have it within our jurisdiction. If the plan was approved by the department, there is no doubt liability on the part of the Dominion to make the improvement.
Has this dam been constructed by the government or by private parties ?
It is a new dam approved of by the government, the building of which has created this need of repairs.

I would think that if the nuisance were created by a dam constructed by private parties, any person aggrieved by that work should have a right of action to recover damages against the parties who constructed it. I can hardly see how the Crown would be called upon to relieve from liability the private individuals who constructed the dam.

There was a suit of Graham against the King, which affirmed the liability of the government because the government had approved of the work which was constructed by private parties. That dam was constructed on the Ottawa river a few miles from the city, and the parties were allowed $3,500 In damages.
The government allowed it to be done ?

There was no liability. The department, and I suppose the Department of Justice as well, thought that the government were liable for allowing it to be done. But outside of legal liability, we have always acted upon the policy that when works were allowed to be done upon navigable rivers that caused any obstruction which did not exist before, it was our duty to make these improvements when such works required them.

I was not aware of any decisions affecting the Crown for having approved of a public work or that, rendered us liable for damages occasioned by the construction of such work. If there are any such decisions I would think it very

advisable they should be carried to a court of appeal. If the court of appeal should determine that we are liable, it seems to me one of two things should be done : Either we should amend the law by providing that there shall be no liability by reason of approving the plans, that any liability shall be confined to the private individuals constructing the work, and that the action for damages shall not be taken away by the fact that the Crown approves the works. Otherwise in every case where works are approved by the government there should be great care taken to investigate the question as to whether those works are liable to lead to any damage for which action could be brought; and in all cases a proper security should be taken from persons constructing the work that they will indemnify the Crown in respect of any such damages. But it seems to me manifestly absurd that the Crown, by reason of approving works which are constructed for the benefit of private individuals, should be liable in damages created by the construction of those works. There is an absolute flaw, either in the legislation or the administration of the department. If a private individual requires the sanction of the Crown for the construction of works to be operated for his private benefit, he certainly should assume all the liability that might accrue by reason of the construction of those works. The duty of the Crown should be confined, I think, to this :	As the works are being
constructed on navigable waters, the Crown should see to it that the erection of those works does not interfere with navigation- that is all the Crown is called upon to do. And I think the statute should be amended so as to provide that the remedy of a private individual against the person constructing the work is not taken away, and at the same time that the Crown, by reason of its approval, is not to be rendered liable for damages so occasioned.

I am informed by the deputy minister that in this case, to which I referred, of Graham against the King, I made a little mistake. The improvements were made by the Crown and not by private individuals. But our idea was that the liability where we approved of them would be the same as if we had done the work ourselves.

There is a large development of trade on the Saguenay river at the present time. The pulp industry alone on that river amounts on an average to 120 tons per day. That is all for foreign shipment. undertaken at an early date. We liope to go on with it next spring, and we ask for this small vote in the meantime to start the work.

That is what we aim at.

This is to make provision for dredging a, channel six miles long, and thirty feet wide and six feet deep at ordinary low water, from the intersection of the canal into Lake St. Francis, with a view to preventing the periodical overflow of lands adjoining the water-course. The total cost will be $25,000.
