I do not quite see how the need for.it arises.

This is in connection with a long standing grievance with the people who live on the shore of the river. The government built a dike along the shore, and in that there is an opening. The proprietor of the mill at the other end of the stream claims this to be his property. I may say that this story is an old one. The difficulty dates as far back as 1837. The government have, at limes, acknowledged the claim and at other times resisted it. The little stream is very shallow, and when the gate is open the lands on both sides are flooded, causing a serious grievance. The proprietor of the mill has taken suit against ilie Crown to have that gate declared to be his property, and that he has exclusive control of it. I do not wish' to commit myself or say anything as to what the result of the suit is likely (o be ; but I have advised that, in case the result of the suit should be in favour of this man, whose name is Robert, it would be wise to make provision to dredge the river. I do not mean to say we are going to lose, but it is wise to make provision.

I quite understand that the hon. minister would not care to discuss the merits of the case, but would it not be well to wait until it is decided before we 422
authorized the expenditure ? Would it not make a difference in the case itself how we view this, matter ?

There have been interlocutory proceedings that are indicative of what is likely to happen. The case has not proceeded because it happens that the judge is on the Pacific coast at this time. If the gate is opened this autumn the results will be very serious. The lands are hay lands, and, if water spreads out and the frost comes, there would be very serious damage to the farmer and very serious cases of damages against the government. The overflow would be by the canal which we built for which we are responsible.
Perhaps I do not quite understand the facts. The gate to which the hon. gentleman refers is some distance away from the property of the owner of the mill ?
The gate is on the side of the river, and then there is a highway and then the land; affected.
Why does he want to open the gate and let the water in upon the lands ?

The mill is immediately below the lands affected, and the water to reach the mill must come down by the stream. He claims that he cannot operate the mill successfully because we keep the gate closed and deprive him of a certain portion of the water.
Perhaps the better way would be to buy the mill.

It is a rather important mill and I need not say to a gentleman of the experience of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) how this importance grows when it comes to a question of the government exercising any claim with regard to any property.

I do not like to commit ourselves without information, and the most important information would be the decision in the suit that the hon. minister was speaking about. It cannot be many months until that will be decided. We have got along without this expenditure all these years, and I do not understand that the state of facts has changed. There may be, perhaps, an increasing damage to the people, but still, that must go on at a very slow rate, as I understand the minister. I do not understand why we should be in such a hurry to vote this money for these improvements until the suit has been decided.

Looking over the papers I find that, as far back as 1891 or 1892, application was made for a petition of right. We took possession of the gate forcibly and keep it closed, and



the petition of right was persistently refused until last year, when it was granted. I cannot say what the result of the suit will be, but I know the opinions that have been expressed by previous judges. And, if the case goes against us, there may be serious damages against the government.
In my own province, under such conditions, the proprietor of a mill flooding the lands of other people would be liable to damages unless he had acquired the right by grant or by prescription.

If the stream continued in its natural course, the lands as they stand would be flooded. As 1 understand-and, no doubt the principle is the same in my hon. friend's province-the proprietor of the mill below would have the right to the flow of water in its natural condition. But the flow has not been in its natural condition for a good many years, and the result is that the proprietors abutting on the river have reclaimed lands on either side. They would have no claim against the mill below if the water flowed in its natural course and flooded lands as it [DOT]did originally before anything was done.
Is this the first item of expenditure for this work ?
Yes.
I notice there is an expenditure of ,$900 last year in this locality.
There are considerable public works there.

Of course, I do not know the length of the flow of the water before it reaches the mill. One would think that if proprietors reclaim land along the bed of a navigable stream they would not have much to complain of. because any man who reclaims land along the stream is bound to raise dikes of some kind to keep the water off the land. Would it not be cheaper, if liability is assumed, to do it that way-building a dike on either side ? Has any Investigation beeu made ?

Yes, the Railway Department have large works and have built a big dike in connection with their works. I do not know whether it is the result of the building of that dike, but that is what is claimed at any rate.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS The officers of the Public W rks Department deny that this is the result of our work.
I had a report made by the engineer of the department and the remedy suggested is the dredging for which I am now asking a vote.
Hon. Mr. iFITZPATRICK.
River du Loup (Fraserville)-harbour improvements. $20,000.

This is a very important point and $250,000 have been spent on this harbour previous to and since confederation. The trade is increasing very much. One of the items in the report of the engineer is that over 20,000,000 feet of lumber was shipped from this wharf during the past year. I am now having an investigation made by the engineers of the department for a large extension of this work, an extension which will probably cost a considerable amount of money under all the conditions. The present vote we are taking for the purpose of making such improvements as we can at the present time. In addition to the 20,000,000 feet of lumber shipped last year there is a considerable general trade.
Who owns the wharf there ?
The government.
Is there anv revenue from it ?
There is a very considerable revenue but I have not the figures here. From my own recollection of the returns of the department I can say that there is a very large revenue.
Would the hon. gentleman explain the nature of the improvements ?

The engineers are now making a general investigation. In a report which my hon. friend may have seen reference is made to tile growing trade on the St. Lawrence and tlie desirability of important improvements being made at one or more ports on that river to afford sufficient facilities for this growing trade. Perhaps my hon. friend did not hear me state that the engineer mentions the shipment of 20,000,000 feet of lumber from that port last year. The Intercolonial road is extended to this wharf and in addition to the lumber trade there is a very large general trade. Until I get the report of the engineers with regard to the whole question of establishing better accommodation on the St. Lawrence, I could not say whether we will go on with these works or not ; that will be for consideration at a future session of parliament. But I may say that the reports, so far as I have seeii them, indicate that the estimated cost of the improvements at Riviere du Loup is between $200,000 and $250,000. However, I am asking for this vote in connection with tlie improvements that are required at the present time.

In what will the improvements consist ; in giving an in-

creased depth of water or the erection of wharfs and accommodation of that kind ?
This is for increasing the depth of water, but some of it will be used in improving the basin and general improvements to the works we have there now.
Will there be dredging ?

Yes, there would be a good deal of dredging if we went on and made the protected basin or artificial harbour of which I spoke. A very large proportion of the estimate I have taken will be used in dredging this artificial basin or harbour. The present purpose is to improve the accommodation for vessels that come to the wharf and to extend the deepwater.
What proportion of the $20,000 would be used in that way ?
I am sorry to say that I cannot give that information exactly. It is a large general work in which a great deal of money has to be spent and the work is not divided.
Is this under contract ?
This is for improvements and repairs which will be done by our own plant.
Is there any contract In relation to any part of it ?
If we went on with all the work there would be, but repairs and dredging immediately necessary we will do with our own plant.
The export is chiefly lumber ?
Chiefly lumber.
Is the lumber sawn at Rivi&re du Loup or is it brought down the river, or it brought there by railway ?
It is brought there by railway.
Riviere du Loup is a prosperous town which has a very import-tant trade. It is the first divisional point on the Intercolonial Railway below Quebec.
What is the population ?

Six thousand. A great quantity of lumber is brought there over the Intercolonial Railway, and especially over the Temiscouata Railway from New Brunswick. The counties of Temiscouata and Kamouraska are tributary to Riviere du Loup, and there are in the neighbourhood important lumbering operations. We have Mr. Fraser at Cabano, who exported last year over 20,000,000 feet of lumber, and we expect that if these improvements are made 4224
at Rivi&re du Loup many firms will send their lumber by the Temiscouata Railway and by the Intercolonial Railway. The Intercolonial Railway has a branch down to the wharf. At the present time there is no accommodation for the vessels coming there and we have to first load the lumber on barges and tow these barges quite a distance from the shore in order to load the vessels. As soon as they have accommodation the vessels can come alongside the wharf, which will save time and money and increase the traffic at Riviere du Loup to a large extent.
What depth of water is there at the present time ?
About six or eight feet.
What depth will there be when the improvements are made ?
They are supposed to give twenty-five feet.

Every hon. member who goes to and from the maritime provinces via the Intercolonial Railway knows that I!ivi&re du Loup is a very important point. My hon. friend the Minister of Public AVorks rather misled me about it, as in the estimate he gives the first half of the name in English and the second half in French, and on behalf of my friends from the province of Quebec, I am going to object to that. I would like to know whether or not the lumber trade is likely to increase ? Are there limits there to supply that trade for a great many years to come ; is it a trade that will develop ? If it is, I think this expenditure would be amply justified.
Mr. GAUA'REAU. A large area of timber limits will be developed by this accommodation, and if we had time to look over the report made last year by the board of trade of Rivi&re du Loup, we would see that it is anticipated that 40,000,000 or 50,000,000 feet of lumber will be exported from this same port.
Why is the word 1 Fra-serville ' inserted in the item ?

It is really the same thing. Fraserville is the name under which the old parish and Riviere du Loup had been incorporated. Rivi&re du Loup is now a town and the name ' Fraserville ' is taken from the old seigneurs who were named Fraser and who were descendants of Colonel Fraser, who was a well-known Hudson bay man in our country.
Sacre-Coeur-wharf, $1,000.
This is in the district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay.
Is it a new wharf ?

It is for a new wharf 210 feet long and 25 feet wide. The intention was to get out the

timber this winter and the total cost of this work when completed will be $8,000.
What is the population ?

I have not the population, but it is in the district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay, which is being settled very fast. There has been a cheese factory erected there, and there is considerable business. The people now have to team their produce to Tadousac over a very bad road.
Is this work to be let by tender and public advertisement ?

Yes.	'
Shegawake-harbour improvements, $4,000.
What is the nature of these improvements ?
This is in Bonaventure, and we have had a petition from the inhabitants. It is undertaken on the report of the resident engineer who reports that a small wharf there would cost $7,000.
This $4,000 is a vote on account.

Yes.
Mr. MAItCIL (Bonaventure). This is situated in the township of Hope, which has a population of 2,411. This township runs along the Baie des Chaleurs for fifteen miles, and the people have no accommodation of any kind in the shape of a landing pier at which to do their business.
What is the nature of the business ?
It is a general lumbering, farming and fishing business, and Shegawake is the most important settlement in that township. It is largely populated by the descendants of United Empire Loyalists.
It is a wonder they didn't build a wharf themselves long ago.

The only wharf In that locality is Port Daniel, teii miles east, or New Carlisle, twenty miles to the west.
Seven Islands-wharf. $25,000.
What is that for ?

This is to make provision for the construction of a deepwater pier on the west side of Bay of Seven Islands. The pier will run out in a northerly direction, nearly at right angles to the shore, and it will have a total length of 4,325 feet, reaching a depth of 48 feet at low water spring tide. The estimated cost is.$65,000. The reason for the work Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
is that there is a most important development going on at that place, and there are now large pulp mills in that district which was up to a year or so ago almost unknown.
Where is it ?
Opposite the west side of Anticosti Island, almost due north.

I have been led to understand that this property is entirely in the hands of a private corporation which has monopolized the whole business, and that they alone will be benefited by the expenditure of this money. A full explanation is necessary, as to how the public interest will be served by this expenditure.

I know something of the Bay of Seven Islands, and of this wharf-partly built by a private company. The deputy minister has just informed me that this bay is six miles long and two and a half miles wide, but it looked to me even more extensive than that, when I was there. The north shore of the St. Lawrence in this locality is now experiencing a wonderful development. As we know, our pine timber in Quebec has practically become exhausted, and our spruce limits are now being exploited. There are no spruce limits in Canada equal to those of the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula.
Nova Scotia comes first.

I will let my hon. friend have his opinion as regards that, but we will still retain ours. There is no objection to a man standing up for his own province. There is only one place suitable for trans-Atlantic shipment from Tadousac down to the Bay of Seven Islands.
Where is it ?
It is a place which Is very well known to the people of the province of Quebec, and which is fast becoming known all over Canada. It is immediately at the entrance to the gulf, opposite Anticosti.
They are building a railway there now.

I was go- [DOT] ing to refer to that. There are very extensive establishments now at the Bay of Seven Islands, but there is no shipping point in the whole of that district. Nature has done more than human ingenuity could possibly devise, to make the Bay of Seven Islands a splendid harbour, and with a comparatively small outlay it can be made perfect for shipping purposes. The entrance is from the west ; it is protected from easterly gales so that it affords perfect accommodation for shipping. The harbour is absolutely landlocked. I do not think I need say more, than that the people who have gone in there

have sufficient confidence in the future of the place, to invest over a million dollars in the erection of important pulp works. When my hon. friend from Grey (Mr. Richardson) says that only one private company will be benefited, I have no doubt he has in mind the Seven Islands Pulp Company, of which Messrs. Meaney and Clarke of New York and Toronto, are the chief shareholders. But in addition to that there are the Boyds, who I think come from Bobcaygeon, Out, and who have large limits in the neighbourhood, and they, to my knowledge own a portion of this bay. I may say that they have applied for a charter for a railway to connect their limits with the Bay of Seven Islands, and in order to accommodate this locality, it is absolutely necessary that we should make this expenditure. '
The limits are on the north side ?

Yes, all on the north side. There are very important rivers there, with very important water-powers. I would ask my hon. friends simply to look at the map and realize that the whole of the north shore of the St. Lawrence from Tadousac down to Labrador is without a single ha.rbour. As they know', the island of Anticosti has for many years borne the name of the graveyard of the St. Lawrence, so numerous have been the wrecks in the neighbourhood of that island. If a vessel is wrecked on th.e lower St. Lawrence, there is nothing to be done but to take her to Quebec or to Halifax. It is of the greatest importance to the navigation of the St. Lawrence that there should be a port in the Bay of Seven Islands, which would be a place of refuge for the vessels, and where they could be repaired. It would be in the public interest to have a wrecking plant and a dry-dock there. It is really more central than Quebec, where there is a wrecking plant now. When a vessel gets aground, it is of the utmost importance that she should be taken off at the earliest possible moment, so as to be saved the consequences of the terrible battering she would get if a storm came on. If a vessel happens to be stranded and is allowed to remain on the rocks for a week, and one of those terrific storms which we have down there comes on, she will, as the saying is, practically pound the bottom out of herself. This place is not in my constituency, but is in the constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Girard); but it is the only point on the lower St. Lawrence where there is a harbour, and it is important that we should have at that central point conveniences for enabling us to go to the help of vessels which may be wrecked in the locality. This work is not for the benefit of one firm only. All those American firms which come in there for the purpose of exploiting our spruce limits will use this port as a port of shipment. How can you ship pulp from the lower St. Lawrence if you
cannot get vessels into a harbour whence it can be shipped ? You have to put it on lighters and send it to some harbour elsewhere; and you cannot ship it in stormy weather at all. If you look at the map, you will see that from the entrance to the harbour of the Bay of Seven Islands there is an absolutely straight line to the other side of the ocean, with nothing intervening; and this port is equally convenient if you want to ship the products south to the United States. So that it has all the natural advantages that a port should have. You cannot expect to have any great agricultural development on the lower St. Lawrence. You may have some mineral development in the future; but there is nothing that I know of in the immediate future except the development of pulp and lumber, and the only harbour from which these can be shipped is the Bay of Seven Islands.
What is the distance from there to Quebec ?
It must be 300 miles.

I eoncur in the view that all these harbours in the St. Lawrence river should be thoroughly exploited. Our whole sea-coast has, in fact, been sadly neglected. But there is a suspicion over here that this is done for the benefit of some private company.

I do not deny that there is one private company, the Seven Islands Company, that is going to benefit very largely. But it will not be benefited to any greater extent than other companies which are in the course of development.
Two years ago I do not suppose there was any person living at that point, while now there are 300 families; and the general development will go on.

I am not concerned about the country not being an agricultural country. The poorest country in the world is an agricultural country, while the country that turns out to be the most valuable is the rocky country. There are parts of Nova Scotia where there is nothing but rock, but it is full of gold. If this is an honest vote for the purpose of serving the trade of the country and promoting its development, then it is desirable; but we do not want any of the public money of this country to be exploited for the benefit of private associations or people with a political pull. The great danger of Canada is that our public money, instead of being used for the benefit of the country, should be pulled away for political purposes; and that must have been the case in the past, for tlm enormous sums of money we have voted in the last twenty years ought to have given us many navigation facilities; yet, so far as

Nova Scotia is concerned, we have scarcely begun to get our seaports into proper condition.
My hon. friends from Ontario know the Boyds, of Bobcaygeon, as one of the largest and most respectable firms in that province; and they know that they are not political partisans of ours.

I know the Mossom, Boyd firm, and I know that, like all other firms of lumbermen, they are quite willing that the government should spend money for their needs in any part of the country. It may be that a harbour of refuge is required at this point. If so. that would he a strong argument for spending the money. But if it is only for the purpose of helping one, two or even three firms that have made investments there in pulp or timber, then I do not think it is altogether defensible. We have a great many men engaged in that line of business in Ontario, and it is a very rare occasion when they apply to the government for a harbour or a dock to enable them to carry on their business. If the hon. Minister of Justice will go along Georgian bay and the Manitoulin islands, he can count the docks by the dozen which have been built by lumbermen for their own needs and in very few instances did they get any aid from the government. Years ago I applied on behalf of some of these to get a. small expenditure made, and I was told that it was not the object of the government, nor did they intend to make expenditure for the purpose of helping private individuals. In cases where there is a harbour or a large town, and where considerable business is done by water, the government may consider themselves justified in spending public money in the general interests, but not for the purpose of helping some one to get out timber who had acquired large lumber limits in the district. There is one instance down here in Quebec, Grand river, where there was an expenditure made for no other purpose than to help a lumbering firm which had acquired timber limits there. After the timber is gone, after the pulp wood has disappeared, what will become of this harbour?

I look up n this particular item as of vital importance. We should develop as much as we can industries in the lower St. Lawrence. The harbour of refuge is the first consideration. and this is the only natural har hour on the whole of that coast.
Is the water very deep ?

Yes, you can float any vessel in it. The deputy minister says it is fifty feet deep. I have gone in there on the ' King Edward.' which is n t a very large boat, but it looked like a small sail boat when we got within the harbour. As a harbour of refuge it is an

ideal place. The industry established at that place is not an ordinary saw-mill, but a manufactory of pulp, and it seems to me most desirable that we should encourage people to come in and manufacture pulp in our own country. In order to get them to do-that, we must provide them with shipping facilities.

After listening to the explanation of the hon. Ministetr of Justice, I am convinced that this vote will do considerable good. The firm mentioned are constituents of mine, and are men of very considerable repute.
Supporters of yours ?

Yes, and this assistance which is given to a large industry is one that should commend itself to the House, more particularly as it will also operate to the advantage of shipping by providing a safe harbour of refuge-.

My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) wras evidently mistaken when he spoke of Grand river as being a place where some public money has been wasted. I presume that he alluded to Grande Vallfie, in the county of Gaspfi. In Grand river there is only an expenditure of *jtSOO provided in the estimates. But regarding Grande Vall6e, I may tell my hon. friend that he is completely in error. The money spent there will be well spent. It is the only harbour on that side of the coast, and I may tell him further that I had no political advantage to gain by this expenditure, because there are no voters of mine there. Although there is a population of 800, these people do not vote, because they are not erected into a municipality.

I know nothing about that ; but I know that at Grande Yallce, the government did not own a foot of land, and had to buy the road to the wharf. There is no settlement there, no village, no shipping interests. But there is a firm which has large timber limits there and which wanted this expenditure to be done for its own purposes. Go to the Manitoulin islands. where there are large limits ; go to Providence bay or to Michael's bay. and-take the other bays along the coast'where large firms are earring on their operations, and not a dollar of public money has been expended to enable them to carry on their business. But at Grande Vallee we find the very reverse. We find the public money expended there for no other purpose than to enable private individuals to prosecute their own enterprises. So far as the present vote is concerned, if this is a suitable harbour of refuge, it is justifiable in my opinion to spend money in order to Improve it. and if there are great industries there, that will be additional reasons, but what we desire on this side is information which will justify us for voting this money.

I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that a company have gone in there to exploit this pulp wood industry and the government is making a grant to them, and to that extent adding value to their property-adding much more value than probably the Minister of Finance understood. The need for a harbour of refuge existed before this company came there, but it was not until this company came to exploit this business that this need for a harbour of refuge began to be felt, and we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that in the estimates the government are making a handsome grant to private enterprise.
Sabrevois wharf-improvements, $1,000.
I notice last year that there was expenditure to complete this wharf for $898. How is it we have another vote this year ?

This is on the report of the engineer, and in a great many of these cases we thought that a certain amount would complete the works. Seven thousand five hundred dollars have been spent on this work already. Where there are large public works, there will be something for repairs from time to time, but wherever work is going on, I am most anxious that we should know exactly the amount. My desire is to change the system so as to inform the committee of the exact amount.

Of course, the engineer could make an estimate showing practically just what the repairs would cost when the expenditure is only about $1,000. I suppose there is only one wharf there, and I suppose that the expenditure of a year ago was made on an estimate showing what it would cost to put the wharf in gcod repair. The Auditor General's Report shows that the expenditure was $998.07 to complete the work. But now again we are asked for a similar amount. The minister will find about the - same with regard to these other small wharfs in this list.
This is mainly for a stone embankment to protect the work.

Why was this not included in the first place ? It appears to me there is a good deal of force in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville) has said. This way of spending money is very misleading to the committee. Last year we voted money supposing that it was all that was required to complete this work. This year we find a call for a further appropriation. To say the least of it, it looks a little suspicious. I suppose the minister acts upon the advice of his engineer, but why should the engineer report in this way? If there is any explanation for making these expenditures in this fashion, we should have it. I am sure that you, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Macdonald), remember how, in years gone by, when the party I support was in power, we heard it often said that the government was spending the people's money to buy the constituencies. I suppose the Minister of Public Works remembers that also. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright),
I am sure, remembers it well. If the late government spent the money to buy up the constituencies, what is this government doing ?
The Minister of Trade and C. mmerce does not hear ytu.

Oh, yes he does. He cannot stay in the House long at a time discussing these estimates, - and I attribute that to the fact that they remind him of the days gone by, when he used to harass the Conservative government.
Get the Prime Minister to work him up.
No ; I am not speaking in that way at all. I do not want to harass the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Prime Minister. I know that in their sober moments
Oh, oh.

I am sorry that hon. members on this side of the House take it so lightly. For my part, I take it very seriously. I feel very much as the Minister of Trade and Commerce felt, no doubt, when he sympathized with the farmers, and said that under an expenditure of $35,000,000 they were being bled white. I would like to hear from the hon. gentleman what the complexion of the farmers is now, when we are voting between $80,000,000 and $100,000,000 for one year. And I do not understand how you can be so pleasant about this matter, Mr. Chairman. But I can understand why you say ' carried ' so quickly over every item. These things must harass your mind, and you do not want to think of how the money is being squandered. When hon. gentlemen opposite used to charge the government that I support with spending the people's money to buy up the constituencies. I sometimes really thought that they -believed there was something in it. Bitt now I see that they must have known that it was a statement made to mislead the public, for we see them supporting a government that has far more than doubled the expenditure. We find one hon. gentleman opposite, one who has attained a venerable age, who gets more money spent in his constituency than any other member in Nova Scotia. I would urge the Prime Minister to consider the result of this lavish! expenditure of the public money. If it goes on, the government will have to borrow to meet the obligations they are entering into this year. I wish the Minister of Public Works would tell us what he means when

he speaks of the report of the engineer. The engineer does not go to a place of his own volition. He goes because he is sent. And, no doubt, he goes with instructions that certain things are to be done and he is to report on them. I wish to repeat what I have said time and again. Neither I nor any other member from Ontario will object to public expenditure on the ground that it is not in our own province. I do not care where the money is spent, so long as it is spent in the best interest of the Dominion as a whole. But I do not think that we are being justly dealt by when wharfs are being built, not only on the Atlantic coast- where, I suppose, there would be a good claim for them-'but on every little river in the maritime provinces and in the province of Quebec. We think we have a right to complain when in a riding like mine, facing on Lake Ontario, which is often boisterous, there are six or seven wharfs, rrd not a single dollar of public money has been spent on any of them. Why, the government is spending $10,000 to supplement the expenditure of a wharf built by a private company. I can understand that the Dominion government Is bound to keep in repair wharfs taken over at the time of confederation, but I say, and no fair-minded man will contradict me, that if these new wharfs are to be built, the people I represent have as good a claim upon the Dominion exchequer for expenditure upon their wharfs as have the residents along the rivers in the maritime provinces and Quebec.

I see that nearly all the other items following this are in the same position as this one-Sorel, Ste. Anne du Saguenay, Ste. Genevieve piers and others. If you turn up the Auditor General's Report, you will find that on these same works small amounts were spent last year, stated to be for the completion of repairs. I cannot believe that in each and every one of these cases the engineer would make the mistake of estimating just about half what the repairs would cost. It looks as if this was merely an annual expenditure in some of these constituencies.

I do not believe the member for the constituency ever knew this vote was to be asked. It is simply recommended by the department, in accordance with the report of the resident engineer, to complete this work.

Last year we voted $1,000 to repair the wharf, and we were told that would be sufficient. This year we are asked for a similar amount. In looking up the Auditor General's Report I see that planking and iron and everything else was purchased for that work. Where the amount is so small we have a right to expect that the department will make a closer estimate. In every case, the repairs Mr. COCHRANE.
should be completely finished by the first vote where the amount is so small.
Mr. LANCASTER, I think there must be something wrong in the engineer's department. I do not see how he could have reported last year that the vote was needed to complete the work, and then make a report this year that the amount was too small, though it is not small in comparison with the amount of work done there.
The only answer I have to make is that last year I had not sufficient money to complete the work.
Then, how do these improvements become necessary?

They are a continuation of the same work. We are raising the structure.
Ste. Anne du Saguenay wharf-improvements.

The purpose of this vote is to substitute a movable slip for the present stairway, which can only be used half the time. This wharf is right opposite Chicoutimi, on the Saguenay.
Ste. Anne de la PSrade-repairs to river bank protection works. $3,000.
This is to protect a portion of the bank of the river against further erosions from the action of the water.

This protection was put on the shore of the Ste. Anne river after that terrible disaster that occurred a few years ago, by which the channel of the river was altered and the river rose to such an extent that it practically carried away the shore at this particular place. It is quite close to the Canadian Pacific Railway bridge, and any one who passes along on the Canadian Pacific Railway can see the situation. In a little more time the action of the river would carry away a part of the shore at that place. This is a navigable river, and is therefore under the control of the Dominion parliament.
Is the Ste. Anne river navigable ?
Yes, at the point where this occurs. I am speaking of Ste. Anne above Quebec.
Should not the province of Quebec look after this work ?

The province of Quebec has no control over it. It is where the Ste. Anne enters the River St. Lawrence. It is practically a basin of the Ste. Anne river.
Ste. Famille-extension of pier, $4,000.

This pier will be 60 by 60 feet and 30 feet high. It is in the county of Montmorency.

This is estimated to be the total cost of the work. It is an extension to deeper water.
This is on the Island of Orleans, below Quebec.
Has this been done by contract ?
The chief engineer tells me this will be under the supervision of the local engineer there.
Why is it not done by contract ? An extension is not like repairing. I can quite understand why repairing might be done by the engineer, but the extension is new work.

If, as my hon. friend says, it is an additional work and specifications can be drawn and contracts let, I would very much rather do it that way.
Ste. Anne de la Pocati6re-reconstruction of pier destroyed by ice shoves, $5,400.

This is to restore the pier which was destroyed by the ice almost entirely. This vote' will' cover the total amount of the cost.
Ste. Anne dj Sore!-repairs to ice piers, $3,800. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. These are repairs to the resistance works or ice piers made on the report of the engineer, and are being done under his direction.
Where are they situated in relation to Sorel ?
Just below Sorel on the St. Lawrence river.
It is near Sorel ?

Yes, quite near Sorel on the St. Lawrence river.
St. Alphonse-Baie des Ha ! Ha !-repairs to wharf, additional amount required, $2,000.

This is for general repairs to the wharf which has been found to be in a deficient state of repair. It is principally for sheeting and planking. There was an appropriation for 1902-3 of $1,500, and this amount is required in addition to that, the total amount of the repairs being $3,500.
St. Godefroi de Nouvelle-breakwater, $6,000. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. This is an entirely new work. It makes provision for a breakwater of cribwork, 700 feet long and 18 feet wide.
Is it in Bonaventure ?
Yes. it is In Bonaventure ; the total estimated cost of the work when finished is $22,000.
Is this at the mouth of (lie Nouvelle river ?

I may say that the citizens of the whole township who are mostly fishermen, have asked for this work. They sent in a large petition at the head of which appeared the name of the Rev. Mr. Leonard, parish priest, an uncle of Mr. Leonard, the hon. member for Laval, and that reverend gentleman asked me to secure the support of that hon. gentleman in regard to this vote. I regret that the hon. gentleman is not at present in the House. This is situated in the township of Hope, in which there Is a population of about 2,400. There are in that place probably 100 fishermen with absolutely no protection. Their only protection is in the Nouvelle river, but that is now almost filled up with sand, so the parish have asked to have this breakwater built one-half mile east of the Nouvelle river. The work is not an expensive one, and it is badly needed by the fishermen who have no protection. This reverend gentleman, Mr. Leonard, mentioned to me the case of three fishermen who had to spend a whole night in open water during a storm, because, having no protection whatever, they were unable to land.
Are there any fishing vessels beyond small boats ?
They are all small boats.
Would it seem to be necessary to build so extensive and expensive a work ?

It appears from the report of the engineer" that owing to the formation of the coast, they have to go out a considerable distance, and the work has to be substantially done, so that it will not wash away with the storms.
If it is only a shelter for small vessels, I do not see why it is necessary to have it of such great length. I can see'that it may be necessary to have it very substantially built.

There is an attendance at the church at St. Godefroi of about 1,200 or 1,400 people. The province of Quebec are opening up townships in the rear of this settlement, and the population is bound, to increase. It increased 50 percent during the last census decade. There is no wharf there now. They have to go out to the open sea in open boats to meet the passing steamers, and they have no way of landing boats or shipping lumber ; in fact there is nothing but what nature has put there. It is hoped that this breakwater will serve the purpose of a landing wharf, where a boat can call, as well as a protection to small boats.

One lion, gentleman asked why it was necessary to go out so far. I think that even with this length of breakwater there will be only between five and six feet of water.
St. Gedeon Islands-wharf. $2,000.
This is to make provision for improvements at St. Ged5on, which is near Chicoutimi, in the district of Saguenay and Chicoutimi The total cost is $6,000.
Is it proposed to do this by contract 7	[DOT]
Yes.
Was there a petition for this 7

1 think the petition was addressed to the hon. member for that locality (Mr. Girard), and by him forwarded to the department. I see that it was. prayed for by the inhabitants. There were three petitions during 1902, and two during 1903, altogether five petitions from the locality.
I would like to ask the minister if there are any districts in Canada from which the government have received petitions to which they have not given heed 7

I am sorry to say that there are a great number. In fact I have stated, and I state now that nearly all of these works are being undertaken on the reports of the engineers of the department in places where ^ they were found to be most urgently needed
St. Fulgence wharf, $1,000.
Where is this 7
This is in the district of Chicoutimi and Snugenay. The total cost will be $6,000.
How far away from the other wharf 7
Seventy miles.
This has been petitioned for 7

Yes.
St. Maurice river-dam at Grand Piles, $10,000. Mr. LANCASTER. What is the explanation of this 7

This is for the construction of a dam 940 feet long at the head of Grand Piles Falls.
A large deputation from the district waited upon me, and I had an investigation made by our engineer, and we came to the cou-elusion that by building this dam we would avoid a large expenditure for dredging, and

that the cost of maintenance of booms, &c., might be reduced at least $20,000 a year. The total cost of this work will be about $65,000. If the engineer is right in saying that this dam will save the necessity for dredging, and will reduce the cost of maintenance $20,000 a year it will be one of the best investments we have made for a long time.
Why should this government maintain these booms ?
For bringing down logs and for the navigation of the river.
The government are not bringing down logs.
No, but we have expended over $1,500,000 on these works.
Do you get any revenue ? The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. We get a revenue of $29,000, which is considerable, but which is nothing in comparison with the cost of the works.

I do not see why the government should object so strongly to government ownership of railways, when they go in for the government ownership of lumber slides. They seem to ly>
very cheer? ful about voting large sums of money'for this purpose.
St. Andre de KaTnoura.ska-extension ot pier and additional repairs, $3,700.
This is to repair damage done by the ice in the spring of 1903, and for the construction of an addition to the pier.
Is it to be done bv contract 7
No, it would be done under the supervision of the local engineer.
What steamers call there ?
I am told that it is principally for schooners.
Are they building schooners to draw a greater depth of water than formerly 7
The explanation is that at present they can only coimj in at high tide and with an extension of 75 feet tliev can get in at low tide.

What are we to understand by the ' local engineer.' These wharfs are 100 miles apart, and we are always told that they will be repaired under the direction of the local engineer. Are we to understand that there is an engineer in every one of these places 7

I should perhaps have said the resident en-

gineer. There is a resident engineer of the department who lives at a central point, and who has supervision over the work in the district. For instance, we have four engineers who reside at Toronto, but they are in charge of the works in different districts of Ontario.

I suppose it is another job like the one we discussed this session; where you have a foreman, and a deputy foreman, and a man to buy material, and about as many officials as you have workmen. These works should not be done by the resident engineer when that can be avoided. There are always a lot of men employed who get large salaries and do very little work. I fancy that the same thing takes place wherever work is done under that rule. Instead of letting a contract for the timber, of which an engineer ought to know how much he wants and have it got out in winter, we generally have a man "to buy timber on commission, a superintendent, a deputy superintendent and a lot of other men putting in their time and drawing a large amount of money, and not doing much work for their pay.

Generally speaking, we are endeavouring as much as possible to let these works by contract. When the engineers do the work, very often a foreman has to be put on, and sometimes better value is obtained in that way than by doing it by contract. But I agree with the hon. gentleman as to the general policy, and we are doing as much work by contract as possible.
St. Fidele-wharf, $4,000.
This is in Charlevoix county. It is for the construction of a wharf for general landing and shipping purposes. It is a new work. The estimated cost is $10,000. It will be let by contract.
Is there not a private wharf near there ?

No.
St. Simeon wharf-extension, $4,000.
This is for the purpose of connecting the present block with the shore, so that boats can land.
Why do you build a block at a distance from the shore?

The water is shallow for a long distance from the shore, and a block is built which serves to accommodate the people. A steamer can tie up at the block, and the people can take their goods to and from it in small boats.
Has the business Increased ?
That is the statement. I have not the-statistics here.
Have you the petition there ?
I have not.

It seems to me that we ought to have some information about this. For some years the people seem to have-got along very well with this block system. Now my hon. friend proposes to connect the block with the land, and he should give-some reason for it.

The reason we have these' blocks is to provide accommodation without a large expenditure of money. Even if there were no increase of business, I think it would be perfectly justifiable to spend this reasonable sum of money in so important a section of the country to connect the block with the land, so that the people will not have to row out in their boats.

That would be a good argument if there were not so many applications for wharfs where there is now no accommodation at all. These expenditures can only be justified on one of two grounds -either that there has been or that there will be a large increase of business.
This block was built in 1889. and the people have been petitioning and Complaining ever since.
This is .on the principle that if you give them an inch they will take an ell. The minister has not given us either of the reasons I have mentioned to justify this expenditure.
My information is that there has been an increase of trade; but even if there had not been, I think we would be justified in providing this accommodation.	.

But in order to do so you have to deprive others who have no accommodation at all, while these people are partially accommodated.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC ,WORKS. I think we are doing pretty well.
Ste. Michel de Belle-ehasse-repairs to pier, $2,500.
This block was sinking, and the vote is taken on the report of the engineer to protect our work. The total cost of the work will be $2,500.

Was there a petition for this, and was each of the names on it certified ?
St. Jean des Chaillons-wharf, $6,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is this a new work ?
This is for the construction of a wharf about three-eighths of a mile below the present ferry wharf. The Lotbiniere and Megantic Railway has a terminal there.
You are evidently making a terminus for a railway. _
The total cost is $28,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: For the benefit of this railway 7
This is the only point where a deep water wharf can be built on that section of the St. Lawrence. It is a terminus of a railway and there is a large trade being done there.
But you have a steamer wharf within three-eighths of a mile, at the end of which there must be deep water.
I understand that that ferry wharf is owned by a private party and does not meet the requirements of the shipping and the railway.

Why should not the railway look after its own requirements ? There is a wharf within three-eighths of a mile, which is a public wharf owned by private parties, if that wharf is not good enough, the railway ought to build its own wharf. Is this new work ?
Yes. The ferry only draws six feet of water, and this is for the purpose of giving fourteen feet of water at this point.
The Grand Trunk Pacific is supposed to supply its own terminal facilities. Why should not this railway ? Between what points does it run 7

From Lyster It extends down to the shores of the St. Lawrence. It was formerly known as the King road, and was practically built for the purpose of enabling the King' Brothers to exploit their large timber limits. The intention is to build this wharf in order to enable the people in that locality to have communication with Quebec and'Montreal. It will serve practically four large parishes. There are very large brick yards there from which the city of Quebec gets practically its whole supply. In addition there is a large mill at that point. Comparisons have been frequently made, with reference to these wharfs, between Quebec and the other provinces, but let me say that to a very large extent the parishes on the river St. Lawrence are deprived entirelv of railway communication. Take the parishes in question. With the exception of that little road which runs back a few miles to Lyster, they are about forty miles from the line of railway, and the river front is the most thickly settled part of our country. The people-have to depend absolutely on the river for communication. These people are not ask-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
[DOT]
ing for much assistance in the way of railway subsidies, and in this locality we have all these parishes absolutely helpless for communication except by water.

We have parishes along the St. John river without railway communication, and depending entirely upon the river to carry their products to market. They have no wharfs built by this government. In some places, I believe, the government has contributed a portion of the cost, the balance being made up by the provincial government. Now. I contend that New Brunswick should be treated in the same way as Quebec, where, as in this case, the circumstances are exactly the same.

I do not know that my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) can compare the two rivers. However, both are important. My recollection is that the Dominion has contributed to a great many wharfs along the St. John. I think I put through a vote this year myself to assist the building of a wharf on 'that river. I think the people on the St. John are better accommodated than those cn the St. Lawrence.

Since the present Minister of Public Works came into office there have been no contributions by the Dominion to wharfs on the St. John. Well, there may have been one. As to comparing the two rivers, I think there will be the same trade on one as on the other.

This part of the St. Lawrence is the most thickly populated part of our province and the most prosperous from an agricultural point of view. And the river is absolutely the only outlet for the trade, unless the people go forty miles back to the railway.
Who owns the railway now 7
I do not know. After James King died it passed into other hands.
Does it not belong to the Grand Trunk 7
No, that runs farther back.
Does not the hon. minister think that, as the railway is as much interested as anybody in having the wharf there, they should contribute to the cost ?

The railway, apparently is very little interested. They regard the competition by water as very serious. If the products of that country could not be exported by water the rate charged by the railway would be prohibitive. The brick yards would then be dependent exclusively on the road. The hon. gentleman can see what the rates would be running over this road to Lyster and on to Montreal or Quebec.

The road must have been built for some purpose, and no doubt, it was to tranship the lumber. The government, in making this expenditure will benetit the railway. Of course, others will get benefit from it also, but it is to the special benefit of the railway to have a wharf there. Surely the railway ought to pay a part of the expense.

I think the railway company will look up: n this as a detriment to them, because it will relieve the people of the locality from the monopoly which the railway would have but for the means provided to use the water transportation. If there is no wharf there, the people are at the mercy of the railway.
Unless I misunderstood the Minister of Public Works there is a wharf there about three-quarters of a mile away.
It is no good, and never can be made of use.
I am a little bit afraid that, if it were not for the government proposing to make this expenditure, the present wharf would be considered very good.
I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) simply wants to learn the facts as they are.
Let me state my case-

I want to say just one word. We on the St. Lawrence are in an unfortunate position because of the rise and fall of the tide. We have these shoals stretching far out from the shore, so that it is difficult to make wharfs. There is a wharf there built by Sir. King, but it is practically useless and cannot be made useful at any reasonable expense.

I understood that the wharf was not a deep-water wharf. But the minister said the principal industry was the manufacture of brick. I. do not think the Minister of Justice will say that it would require a deep-water wharf to ship brick, because, I am satisfied those brick would be carried in barges. Here in Ottawa during the present session I have seen them again and again unloading brick from barges. Let me draw the minister's attention to the case of another wharf which I have in mind. The Central Ontario Railway runs back into the country, in Hastings county, and when a terminal wharf was wanted for that road the company built it at their own expense. I am satisfied that the brick will be carried in barges and not in steamers. Is not that correct ?
Yes.

I sympathize with the people there, if they are without facilities to ship their products, and, I am willing to give my vote for the expenditure of public
money to provide these facilities where necessary. But I do not want to vote money to build a deep-water wharf for the accommodation of an industry if there is a wharf already there at which the products can be shipped.
I would point out to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) that we are spending a good deal of money In the province of Ontario to help to provide terminals for railways.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: In the absence of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Calvin) I wish to make one more appeal to the hon. minister on behalf of the residents of Wolfe Island and Howe Island. There we have two municipalities situated at the foot of Lake Ontario. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (lit. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) knows all about them and can verify all I say. These two municipalities include a large population, yet the people have no opportunity to leave the island except by ferry, and I do not think the government have ever spent a dollar in building or maintaining a wharf in either of them. I think it quite time the Minister of Public Works should look into this matter, and I trust he will send his engineer to inquire, and that next year we shall find a sum in the estimates for a wharf there. I think that Ontario is entitled to something and the inhabitants of these islands should receive attention.
Is this where we are doing the dredging V

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes. '

I will take a note of it and have the inquiry made.
Yamaska lock-dredging below lock, $8,000.

This estimate is asked for by the resident engineer, for dredging the River Yamaska below the Yamaska locks, to a depth of six feet. This river takes its rise in the county of Brome, and after a course of about 90 miles, empties into the St. Lawrence eight miles above the town of Sorel. It is a navigable river.
Department of Public Works-to provide for arrears of salary due to the chief architect, November 1, 1897 to June 30, 1903, at $3,200 per annum, together with $200 short-estimated in his salary for 1903-4, $1,333.33.

This is to pay arrears of salary due to the chief architect between the dates mentioned. The chief architect, Mr. Ewart, has been employed in the department since 1871. On the superannuation of Mr. Fuller he was appointed to the position at a salary of $3,200 per year, but he was never paid the full amount of his salary up to the present year.
Why.
I do not know why. It has been going on, and never was made right. This is to pay the balance due him.
It is not usual for men to let their salaries remain unpaid like that.

This gentleman is one of those peculiar men who do not look carefully after their own interests, for he did let it lie all these years. He is entitled to it*as a matter of law, and be never got his increase. He is a very tine old gentleman.

Does the hon. gentleman think it is a sign that he is a very good servant if he does not look after his own interests better than that ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS It means that he was looking after public business more carefully than after his own.
To say that he has been neglecting for six years to draw $200 a year coming to him is more than I can understand. It is strange that the department knew nothing about it.
I did not say that. I said that as a matter of fact he only drew $3,000 a year, whereas he was entitled to $3,200 a year from the time he was appointed chief architect up to date.
I am afraid he is not a very good architect of his own fortunes.
It is so extraordinary that one can scarcely consider it witli patience. It looks so absurd that a man should allow this to be going on for six years and did not know enough to ask for it.
I do not say that he did not know it. All I can say is that, as a matter of fact, the books show that he never drew his full salary.
I think his action is highly commendable. It strikes me you ought to pay him interest on the arrears that he has allowed to accumulate.

He ought to suffer the loss of interest for his mistake.
Department of Public Works-salaries-to promote Mr. J. B. Hunter to a first-class clerkship notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. $300.
Mr. Hunter is private secretary to the minister, and has proved a very hardworking, capable man, as every person admits. His present salary is $1,100.
How many private secretaries has the minister ?
I am sorry to say I have only one.
I must commiserate the minister if he has only one secretary. Evidently he is more modest than the Minister of Inland Revenue, who, I believe, has now three and an assistant.
What has been done with the others ?
I will have a private conference with the hon. gentleman if he wants to know further.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No. 140, the Yukon.	.
We want to know what the salaries are before that is called.

My hon. friend will see that from the increased amount of work done in the department there must necessarily be a greatly increased expenditure for printing. Ail these specifications have to be printed; this is not for newspapers.
I understood the hon. gentleman to refer to newspapers.

The subscriptions to newspapers have not increased. I understood my hon. friend to ask what had increased, and I was giving the principal items of increase. Printing, stationery and telegraph charges have increased owing to the increased number of works, and the greater number of men in the employment of the department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I will have to ask this other Yukon item to stand; the hon. leader of the opposition is not present, and he will have something to say on this question. My hon. friend behind me will also have a statement that he will have to make either now or on concurrence, and I think it would be well to have the item stand.

My hon. friend has made out a rather bad case, for I would rather put this through when these gentlemen are away. While I was anxious to get through. I must say that the opposition have treated me with a great deal of courtesy, and at their request I shall certainly allow the item to stand.
Some resolutions reported.
