to move from this side of the House, will not he moved until a later- date.

Motion agreed to, and House went into [DOT]Committee.
To provide for a grant to the Toronto Industrial Exhibition Association, to assist in the holding of a National Canadian Exhibition, in Toronto during the present year, 1903, $50,000.
['Owing to the absence of some members who wish to discuss the matter, the motion which it was intended\n\nto move from this side of the House, will not he moved until a later- date.']
Was not this amount voted last year ?
No. It was agreed to by the government at an early period of the session, that it would be put into the supplementary estimates.
Was it not decided last year to give this money ?
Yes, but there was never any vote taken for it. The exhibition took place within this fiscal year.
Were there any conditions attached to this vote ?

Yes, the Order in Council explains the conditions. This is a letter which was written to the exhibition authorities under date of March 31st:
I have the honour by direction of the acting minister to inform you that an Order in Council has been passed, granting an amount to the Toronto Industrial Exhibition to assist in the holding of an all-Canadian exhibition in Toronto during the present year; such grant to be applied to the following purposes; first, to equalize freight rates for exhibitors. Second,, special and extraordinary prizes. Third, advertising outside the province of Ontario. Fourth, the cause of securing and maintaining an educational exhibit, and fifth, the increased cost in the management.
After the exhibition, I wrote to the authorities and asked them to give me some information as to the manner in which they had arranged to apply this money. 1 received the following details from Mr. Orr, manager and secretary of the exhibition -company :
The estimate under the headings named which was given to the government at the time the application was made will be approximately correct and is as follows :
Equalization of freight rates for exhibitors $15,000 ; special and extraordinary prizes, $14,000; advertising outside Ontario, $9,090 ; securing and maintaining educational exhibits, $8,000; increased cost of management due to the increased length of time the exhibition was held, and fine arts exhibit, $4,000, total, $50,000.

The reason I made the inquiry was, that one of the Toronto papers stated that this grant had not all been used, and that it was intended to return about $13,000 to the government. 1 was surprised. It displayed a magnanimity and an honesty that most corporations usually do not get credit for. However, I fully endorse tills grant. It did a great deal of
good, and I believe the exhibition was a great deal better than usual. I am sure it would be much appreciated if the grant were continued from year to year.

I hardly think we could promise that, because the Dominion government has not | been in the habit, for a number of years l back, of granting any help to local institutions, but this was an extraordinary occasion. The exhibition was very much better, I believe, than it had been for many years, or perhaps ever before. I think the grant accomplished the object aimed at.
Further amount required for fumigating stations. $500.

Why are we not able to estimate the cost of this in your main estimates, without spreading it over two or three votes ? It would require no very high degree of discernment on the part of the medical health officer, to calculate the amount he would need for this purpose.
This is for the fumigation of nursery stock.
Why are you not able to make your calculation in the main estimates ?

Last year we found our estimates had been exceeded, and we had to ask a supplementary estimate. We have to make provision for the same increase in expenditure tills year. It has been found that in British Columbia they can import nursery stock all through the winter, and as they have asked that their stations should be kept open for a longer period in the year than is the custom in the east, this increase is almost entirely due to that reason. In other stations we have had to pay a little higher for labour.
What has been the success of this system in keeping out the San .1 os6 scale V

The prohibition of the importation of nursery stock has kept the San JosS scale out of Canada, and the fumigation stations were a concession to the trade, so as to allow the importation of nursery stock at certain designated ports. I do not think there is any doubt that fumigation as carried on at these stations has been completely successful.
I saw a statement to the contrary some time ago in a paper. I forget what paper it was. It stated that some of the stock showed evidences of being affected after it was growing.

No such statement has been brought to my attention, and no complaint of that kind has ever come to the department. In the agricultural and horticultural press, where

I suppose we might expect to see such statements, nothing of the kind ever appeared.
How many of these stations have we to-day, at how many places is stock allowed to be brought in, and what is the aggregate cost of this work ?

The aggregate cost, with this supplementary vote, will be $3,000 a year. The stations are at Vancouver, B.C., Winnipeg, Man., Windsor and Niagara Falls, Ont., St. Johns, P.Q. and St. John, N.B. At each of these places we have a small house for fumigating purposes and a man in charge. He has to employ day labour occasionally when a large consignment comes in.
Further amount required for archives, $3,000.
What is this for ?

This is an addition to what we have already had for the archives in years gone by. It is required to provide for an entirely new arrangement of the work. Some four years ago a report was made to council by a commission of officials who were appointed to investigate the condition of our records and our state papers. That commission reported that there was| an immense mass of historical and other records of various kinds scattered through the various departments, that they were in a dangerous condition, and that a new arrangement ought to be made for their collection, care, classification and cataloguing. For one reason and another, chiefly because it was quite impossible to ask the late archivist, Mr. Douglas Brymner, at his time of life, to undertake a new work of that kind and reorganize the department, nothing was done ; but on the occasion of his demise and the consequent vacancy in the position of archivist, I drew up a memorandum to council recommending certain changes in the archives branch. These would involve a considerable addition to the work and the responsibility of the officer in charge, and would involve his having some assistance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who is in charge ?

Nobody is in charge. No appointment has been made to the vacant position. The change would necessitate considerable work in the way of collecting these documents and records which are scattered through the different departments, and which we wish to bring together under a responsible officer, whose duty it will be to care for them, watch over them, study them, make extracts from them, and compile them for the report on the archives. I have no hesitation in saying that in the interest not only of the history of our country, but the safety of our records, this work is necessary. To show the danger and the necessity of some such work, I may mention that some years Hon. Mr. FISHER.
ago, by the order of a certain officer of the Militia Department, a number of boxes which appeared to contain waste paper were taken out of a room in the Militia Department and put in the furnace. It was afterwards found that in these boxes were a large number of important military plans and other papers of the greatest value from a historical and departmental point of view; and they had all been destroyed by people who were really not responsible, and had no right to act in that way. There has been abundant opportunity for that kind of thing to occur at any time in a number of our departments, and I think it is quite time that these important documents should be brought together and classified and catalogued and put into the charge of a responsible officer of sufficient standing.
It would not be amiss if you extended the same protection to the ballots in Ontario.
Who is the chief clerk now at the head of that department V

The branch is under the charge of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, along with all the other branches of the department. The clerk who has charge of the documents at present is a Mr. Duff, who has been for many years under the archivist.
I noticed a few days ago in one of the papers published in Ottawa that Mr. Casey, the late member for West Elgin, was to be appointed to that position.
No appointment has yet been made, and no decision has been come to in regard to it.

I notice that in 1892-93 we voted $8,000 for the archives : in 1893-91 we increased the vote to $9,000 ; andi now it is proposed to further increase it to $12,000. I cannot understand why it should be necessary to have a part of this item in the main estimates and a part of it in the supplementary estimates. It is not a matter in regard to which there can be any unusual demand created which could not be known at the time the main estimates are prepared. To divide the item in this way doubles the work in the House, and makes the matter less understandable. We have to make an inquiry into two items instead of one. thus virtually doing the work twice over.

There is a good deal in what the bon. gentleman says, but in this particular instance the circumstances are different. The item in the main estimates was sufficient for the old work, but there has been a change made. It was only since I came back from Japan that I secured the consent of my colleagues to the change or the whole amount would have been in the main estimates.
Then the hon. gentleman got this new idea in Japan.
I did not say that.
I see there is a vacancy, Mr. Brymner having died. Is it intended to fill that vacancy ?
I hope so, hut I did not wish to fill it until I had the assurance that these changes would he agreed to.
Is that the position reserved for our late colleague, Mr. Casey ?
It is not reserved for anybody.

I may say that if Mr. Casey is qualified-and I have no doubt he is-I would he glad, and I have no doubt that a great many other lion, members would be glad, to see him get it. I think many less deserving men have got positions. In my opinion, our late colleague, Mr. Casey, would be eminently fitted for the position, both on account of his literary qualifications and general ability.
Further amount required for Archives, $3,000.
What progress has been made with this work ? It is a very interesting subject to us in the maritime provinces to trace the families who came from France.

I can only say that Mr. Gaudet, who is in charge of the work, reports that he is making steady progress. He has been travelling in the maritime provinces to' secure data and lately he has been working at Ottawa compiling that data for the volume to be issued. It is a work in connection with the Acadian families, somewhat similar to the work of the late Abb6 Tanguay with regard to the French Canadian families of the province of Quebec. It will give information with regard to the lineage, genealogy and origin of the Acadian families in the maritime provinces. This item would not have been in the supplementary estimates had it not been inadvertently omitted from the main estimates.

I take great interest in this matter. Mr. Gaudet has got all the information necessary to have the first volume issued with the exception of some information regarding a couple of censuses, which cannot be obtained in this country and which he is securing in Paris. Upon receipt of this information from Paris, the first volume will be completed, and be shortly in the possession of the public. Mr. Gaudet has assured me that he thinks he will be able, between this and next spring, to have the first volume published. The first volume is the- most difficult. He has all the material and data prepared for the issue of the second and third volumes. There will be in all probability about four volumes, and each will 423
follow the other very rapidly as soon as the first is published.

While I have no special < bjection to this work. I fail to see why we should collect information about the Acadian families any more than about the English, Irish, Scotch, German or any other nationality. I do not see why parliament should vote money for keeping a work of that kind going on which will practically go on for ever, because when you start a work of that kind it rarely ever stops. It is like a pension, the recipient of which lives a very long time. Why this work should be done for one nationality any more than another is what I cannot understand.

I must object to the remarks of the hon. gentleman. The hon.
gentleman and myself are both descendants of the old Irish race and we are proud of it.

Do you want a record of
your genealogy '!

We have a record. What we are seeking to obtain is a genealogy of the old Acadian people, the first settlers of the eastern provinces, and it seems to me that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is not exhibiting that broadness of mind which should distinguish a descendant of the race to which he and I belong when he objects to this work. I would like to ask the hon. minister if Mr. Gaudet is still in charge of that work and has he made any report ?
Yes, Mr. Gaudet is in charge of the work, and he has reported verbally from time to time, but there is no published report.

Do I understand from the hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is an Irishman. That is something new to me. I always understood that the hon. gentleman from East Grey came from' Scotland.

It is a strange coincidence but the hon. member for East Grey had the same impression with regard to the hon. member for Montreal. But I have to say in reply to my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island, who complains that a man is not very broad in his views who objects to this expenditure, that I think the breadth of view of the hon. member for East Grey will compare favourably with that of the hon. member from Prince Edward Island, as regards anything pertaining to the welfare of the country. If it be the aim of parliament to set apart a portion of money for the purpose of tracing the history and the record of the different nationalities of this country, I have no objection. But I ask, why select the Aca-dians in preference to the others ? While



I have no objectim to the [DOT] Aca-dians-on the contrary my acquaintance with them leads me to the conclusion that they are a very estimable people-I fail to see why this work should be done for them any more than for the II. E. Loyalists, who came to this country and who are reputed to be the pioneers of this continent, and whose name stands so high in the history of the world to day.
Why not do it for the U. E. Loyalists ?

That is what I say. If it is desirable to do it for one nationality, why not for the other, and to make a selection of one seems to me like partiality. I am not objecting to this, provided it is thought desirable to carry it out with regard to any celebrated class in the country who have a notable history. But what I object to is the fact that one nationality is selected and all others ignored. That is what I cannot understand or regard as just.
When may we expect the first volume of the work ?
I think it is expected about next spring.
How much has been expended oh it up to date ?
This item of $1,400, being $1,200 for salary and $200 for travelling expenses for the gentleman in charge, has been voted for three years.

With regard to the remarks that the hon. member for Montreal, St. Anne (Mr. Gallery) made. I may say that if he wished to discover a Scotchman in the House he has only to look in this direction. I am at a loss to understand why a distinction should be made between nationalities in such a grant, as is being done.

As that point has come up again, I would like to correct the hon member from West Prince (Mr. Hackett). I distinctly state that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is not an Irishman. If I understood him aright, the hon. member for West Prince said that the hon. member for East Grey was an Irishman.
I insist on the fact that the hon. member for East Grey is an Irishman, and just as good an Irishman as the hon. member for Montreal, St. Anne.

If I understand the meaning of the word ' Irish ' as used in the north of Ireland, I would say that the hon. member for East Grey is not Irish, according to the strict use of the word. And so I think the hon. member for Montreal, St. Anne, is quite correct. If in Ireland today, the hon. member for East Grey would repudiate the designation of ' Irish ' as applied to him.

I think, since this seems to be a disputed question, that we had better have another branch of this inquiry to determine' the genealogy of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Anne, aud myself, and determine to what nationality we belong.
Further amount required for renewing and improving Canadian exhibit at Imperial Institute. London, $5,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before this item is discussed, I have a matter I wish to bring before the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. It is not quite apropos of the item, but there was a matter brought to my attention in a letter which I handed to the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn). That hon. gentleman is not in his seat and I have not the letter, so I can only give the information I have. First I would inquire if Mr. J. G. Anderson is an inspector of fruit in the Department of Agriculture ?
He is. I answered that question yesterday.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The information I have is to this effect-that this gentleman who is inspector of fruit and drawing pay from the government, is also an apple buyer aud speculator, and ships apples every day to the market at Ottawa. These are facts I know. The statement is made that he will go to a farmer to purchase his fruit, aud, if the farmer does not sell to him at his own price but sells to another speculator, Mr. Anderson is brought in to inspect the fruit aud cuts him down to the last point. And so the farmers of Prince Edward are under compulsion to sell to Mr. Anderson. That is the statement made in this letter from one of the large dealers in Ottawa, and now in possession of my hon. friend from Prince Edward.

This is the first I have heard of such a charge. I know nothing about it. Mr. Anderson was a dealer in fruit before he was appointed inspector. When he was appointed he had to close out his business and cense carrying on any trade of that kind. If he is dealing in fruit he must either cease doing so or cease to be inspector. My inspectors cannot for a moment be allowed to deal in fruit or to have anything to do with the trade.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The writer of this letter says that Mr. Anderson is shipping apples to Ottawa every day in the week, and he is his own inspector.
I will inquire into that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Anderson is a very strong supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite and an electioneering agent through the country, and he must draw a salary in order to keep in the field. Yet,

he is making his profits out of purchasing apples.

All I can say is what I have already said- that this is the first I have heard of this allegation, and with all due deference to my hon. friend's informant, I do not believe it. But I will make inquiries. And, as I said a1 moment ago, no inspector in my department is, or can be, allowed to deal in fruit. I will investigate the matter and secure the information.
What is the object aimed at in this Canadian exhibit at the Imperial Institute in London V

The older members of the House will remember that a good many years ago, at the time of the Queen's jubilee, the Imperial Institute was established in London, specially for the purpose of having an exhibit of colonial industrial products. Propositions were made to the Dominion government to secure their co-operation. The institution was then under the patronage and presidency of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the present King. The arrangement come to at that time was that the provincial governments should deal with their respective exhibits in the Imperial Institute in London, the Dominion government taking no pai't. This went on for many years, but complaints began to arise and were voiced in this House by hon. members on both sides who said that the Canadian exhibits in the institute were not at all creditable to the country. The High Commissioner iu London made very strong representations to the government on the question, and asked that some thing should be done to improve the character of the exhibit there. I was over in London some few years ago and visited the institute. On so doing, I fully concurred in the view that the exhibits of Canada's products there were entirely inadequate and not creditable to Canada. After a good deal of discussion, I asked for a small item in the estimates to improve those exhibits. That was granted me to the extent of $3,000. Almost immediately after the vote was given the imperial authorities undertook to reorganize the Imperial Institute. It had been under the control of a royal commission of eminent people of the old country who were specially interested in it and who had been invited to take part in its management by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and joined with them were colonial representatives, including the High Commissioner for Canada, at first Sir Charles Tupper and afterwards his successor Lord Strathcona. Tile different Canadian provinces have had each a representative. Speaking from memory, I think that three of the provinces asked Lord Strathcona to act as their representative, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and perhaps some other provinces had their local 423*
representative in England. The institute, I may say, had been getting into disrepute and! had almost failed of its object, and the imperial authorities, after consultation with the various representatives of Australia, South Africa, New Zealand and Canada, decided on a change. It took a long time to carry that change through, and for two years back the fate of the Imperial Institute has been hanging in the balance. This last winter, after the main estimates were submitted to this House, Lord Strathcona sent out a communication to us explaining that at last the institute has been taken over by the Imperial Board of Trade, which is the department corresponding to our Department of Trade and Commerce, and that in the future the Imperial Institute was to be managed as a branch of the Board of Trade, but with the concurrence and co-operation of the different colonies. They proposed some additional work in the shape of a city branch. I ought to say perhaps for the information of those who are not familiar with it, that the Imperial Institute is located at South Kensington, in the part of London where the great exhibition of 1862 took place, quite out of the business part of the city, although it is a place where there is a large number of museums and educational establishments. The new organization and management propose to have a city office with show-rooms and accommodation for a library and reading rooms. In addition to that they have asked the various colonies to fit up the exhibits in the institute proper in South Kensington, on a grander and better scale, and completely to renovate the exhibit.
Now, this work seems to fall naturally into the exhibition work of my own department, and when Lord Strathcona's communication was received by the government here, after careful consideration, we concluded it was in the interest of Canada to be worthily and properly represented in that institute, and we propose to carry out the scheme as submitted by Lord Strathcona, after discussion with the authorities of the institute. That scheme involves a slight increase iu the expenditure of the ordinary work of the institute, and an increased subscription to the city office, and the employment in addition of a caretaker, of a stenographer or clerk, who will be able to reply to correspondents and to be present, either at the west end institute building or in the city alternately with the curator himself. This office expenditure which we are asked to agree to by the imperial authorities involves an expenditure of about $6,000 a year. I propose to ask altogether for $8,000, $2,000 to be devoted to preparing, sending and installing the characteristic exhibits of Canadian products. Six thousand dollars will not be all, because Lord Strathcona, as the representative of the different provinces, is asking them to continue their contribution to the general expenditure of the exhibition,

and in that case there will be a sum of money available out of the sum I am asking, to arrange for the permanent exhibits, and also to arrange for the temporary exhibits of a particular character. The main estimates for the current year included a sum of $3,000 for this Imperial Institute, the same as we have had for two or three years back, and I ask this $5,000 additional to make the $8,000 which will be necessary to carry out the scheme outlined by Lord Strathcona.
What will be the nature of these exhibits ?

I have a memorandum which Lord Strathcona sent out here in which he says in regard to that:
The scheme is for the arrangement and reorganization of the exhibits in the South Kensington building of the institute. Visitors will in future be assisted in getting information by special demonstrations in the courts, by means of pamphlets and other printed information systematically distributed, and also by public lectures.
6. It is understood that a number of the colonies are in favour of placing the responsibility for the care, maintenance and renewal of their collections-at the expense of the colonies-on the authorities of the Imperial Institute, who would of course be in close communication with the respective colonial governments on these subjects. The Canadian collections now need complete renewal and numerous additions to make them thoroughly representative of the country, and no doubt the Imperial Institute will if desired, be prepared (in conjunction with the curator) submit a scheme for this work, and to explain how it is proposed- to carry it out.
He goes on to explain what has been in the past, and then be says :
I understand that a special staff is to be appointed by the hoard of trade, in connection with the collections, so that their care and maintenance shall be continually attended to. This arrangement would set the Canadian officer (now-termed the curator) free from much of the routine work, and would enable him to devote himself almost exclusively to answering the inquiries addressed to the Canadian section, and to supplying information to intending emigrants and commercial men. The collections at the Imperial Institute might be further utilized with great advantage by our own emigration department for the purpose of illustrating the general natural resources and industries of the Dominion. The board of trade propose to amalgamate their own commercial intelligence department now at Whitehall, with the office established by the Imperial Institute in the city of London, where additional premises will be taken.
Then he goes on to say that the colonies will have an opportunity to occupy offices in that building. One part of the exhibit will be in the commercial city of London and the other in this west end place.
Why is it desirable to have two ?

To accommodate the .larger exhibit in the Hon. Mr. FISHER.
city would require an enormous expenditure to get sufficient room. The building is a very large one, and it would require an enormous expenditure to transfer that to the city and to procure the accommodation required for these exhibits. They wish to have what may be called a business branch in the city, at which information may be given and temporary and partial exhibits can be made of particular articles at particular times. It is taken from the west end branch or part of that supplied temporarily. I would suggest that we in Canada could very properly take one of the rooms in tiie city branch and from time to time make exhibits of different Canadian products. For instance, at one time we could have an exhibit of dairy products, butter and cheese, another time an exhibit of bacon, at another time of dressed poultry, at another time of minerals, or of some particular mineral with which Canada is particularly favoured. Then we might make an exhibiit of certain manufactured g ods which we thought we might be able to induce the British people to buy. These exhibits would be temporary, lasting perhaps a week or two weeks. These exhibits could be especially advertised and special invitations could be sent to those engaged in trade in the particular product which might be ou exhibition. That is the object in keeping the city office in addition to maintaining the reading rooms and supplying information to business men in the city who have not time and who would not take the trouble to go to South Kensington to make inquiries, hut who would call at a room or building in the city of London.
That would mean a dual set of officers.
Has the hon. gentleman seen the building ?

I have seen the Kensington building, but

not the city offices, I do not think they are yet taken. When Lord Strathcona was! here, about a month or two ago, they had not yet engaged or acquired any city office.
In what part of Whitehall will the building be ?

It will not be in Whitehall ; it will be down, in the city in the neighbourhood of the Royal Exchange. Last year, or the year before, we had a temporary city office in Eastclieap, which is a little east of the Royal Exchange, but I understand from Lord Strathcona that they have given that up and are going to get larger and better rooms.
Then I understand that these exhibits will consist of the natural products of the soil, the forest and the mine ?
And industrial products as well.
Have you provided for large maps to be displayed in these buildings, so that the people may understand the geography of Canada ?

I have not yet made any definite plan in that respect. We have to-day in my department a large map which was exhibited at Paris, and which I think is now in London, and that map could be utilized. In fact I gave orders a little while ago that that map should be kept in London for the purposes of the Imperial Institute. It is a very fine map of the Dominion of Canada.
It would be a good plan to show on that map the unoccupied lands in Canada adapted for cultivation and settlement.
That is shown on the map.
I would ask the minister if there is anything in this exhibit to demonstrate what progress Canada is making in the fine arts 1
We have not any fine art exhibit there ; it is an exhibit purely of what I might call the natural and industrial arts of the country.

I wish to offer a few- remarks on a subject that is perhaps germane to this question. Wre have in this city a gallery of fine arts, so-called. It is entirely unworthy of this country, and of this city, and some provision ought to be made with the view to procuring a better exhibit of the works of Canadian artists. Canada has already found a place in the appreciation of the artistic world beyond the confines of this country. Canadian art is recognized in the United States, and has had very favourable notice from American
critics, while we at home seem to be less appreciative than we should be of what our artists are doing and struggling to do. The fine arts can make progress in any country only by having some reasonable patronage, either from the wealthy people of the country or from the government. Art has made the greatest progress where it has had the support and patronage and recognition of governments. I notice that several new pictures have been added to the collection at the old rookery in Ottawa which we call an art gallery, and on inquiry, I have been informed that some $7,000 have been expended in the purchase of pictures, the culls of the studios of the old world, which could not be disposed of there and which have been sold through some medium to the Canadian government. I am not an art critic, but I have been privileged to see some of the rarest collections of art in the old world, and I am bound to say that we have in the gallery some work of Canadian artists which is worthy of a place in any art gallery in the world. But there are some very meritricious works in our gallery, and I fear that some works have recently been added at a large expense which could have been bought from some picture dealers by people who know how to go about it, for perhaps from $10 to $20 each. How they have added to the collection in this city to the extent of $7,000, I fail to see, while the works of Canadian artists have been passed over without recognition or notice. I am sure that we have occasion to be proud that we have in this young country- for we are still a young country-such a development of artistic taste and ability as has taken place in Canada in the last eight, ten or fifteen years. We have in Canada men who have made for themselves a place in the old world ; a picture by Paul Peel in our gallery is worthy of a place in any art gallery in the world. We have such names as Homer, Watson, Cote, Verner, Harris, Krieghoff, Gauthier, Forbes, Brownell, Sherwood, Bell, Smith, in Ontario and Quebec, while in British Columbia we have working Mower Martin, a man who has contributed a great deal to Canadian art. In Nova Scotia we have Mr. Miles, and then in New Brunswick we have an artist whose name I cannot now recall, of whom a well known art critic in America has said that if he were selecting the three greatest artists in America he would not omit his name. I think the time has come when these men should have some fair consideration. It is thought by some that in the rural districts, among the toilers of the country, there is not that recognition of art there should be ; it is felt that they do not consider art and attach importance to it. I can tell the House that this is not so, and that importance is attached to art in this country, and there is a budding and steady growth and development of artistic taste. In this connection T will reJ

1351ft
late a little Incident that came in my own expei'ienee. I was looking over some fine Christmas cards in a shop just before Christmas, when a man came in with whom I entered into conversation. I said something about their being beautiful, and he said : Well, there is great waste of money in these things. I said : Do you think so; have you no love for pictures ? He replied-None at all; I suppose there are hundreds of dollars spent on these things, I told them that there were tens of thousands of dollars spent on them, and he said that it was a terrible waste of money. And I said to him : You have no appreciation of pictures or of the beautiful; I have never seen where you live, but still I can tell you what it is like; if you come to it on a June day you will see thistles and weeds growing in the fields and between the fences; you will see no avenue of shade trees, leading from the roadway to your house, and if they were there you would cut them down for firewood; you will see no flower beds ornamenting your garden; nothing of the beautiful; if your buildings have any paint at all the colours are inharmonious and incongruous; your farm is cultivated in a slovenly manner; your fence corners are filled with weeds, and your outbuildings are in a ruinous condition. He said : That will do, I do not want to hear any more. I had the fortune to be passing by his place some time afterwards, and when my companion told me who lived there, I said : Turn in, I want to have a look at it. I went up to the door of his house and he met me, and he recollected the picture I had drawn. It was too true. Nature has placed us in a grand country. We have the means of making Canada a place of paradisiacal beauty. It only needs the development of the artistic faculty to make our roads, our fields, our homes and everything about us beautiful. There are no more beautiful trees in the world than the Canadian maple, which we have chosen as our national emblem. No one can travel through Canada at this season of the year without feeling that it is a constant panorama of beauty, unequalled in any part of the world. We only need a recognition of the artistic taste which I believe we have in this country. We need our fellow countrymen who have sufficiently advanced their artistic taste to be genuine critics in this respect, should bring into our art galleries these Canadian paintings which are worthy to be in any art gallery in the world. We should have art centres in every large city in Canada, and we should make our native art accessible to our young Canadians. It is not a useless expenditure: it is an expenditure which will redound immensely to the credit of all Canada.
Hear, hear.
I cannot refrain from thanking the hon. gentleman {Mr. Richardson) for his appro-

priate and eloquent address. Unfortunately I cannot act upon the suggestions he has made, but I will draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works, in whose department the matter is, to the remarks of my hon. friend. I appreciate very highly what he has said with reference to our Canadian artists. We have a group of men, and I may say of women too, whose art works exhibited in the art centres of the old country, would attract attention even amongst the best. The hon. gentleman has given us a list of the greatest Canadian artists, and I have no doubt there are others whose art will confer credit on this country. I endorse what the hon. gentleman has said with reference to the art gallery in Ottawa. We have pictures there worthy of any gallery.
I recognized a picture there the other day by Paul Peel to which this remark would apply, and right alongside it is a picture of a young Canadian, by Mr. Robert Harris, which was presented by a lady of Ottawa, and which shows the true characteristics of the young Canadian of whom we are all so proud. There have been one or two pictures added to the gallery lately which are certainly most creditable. The picture by Ten Kate is a splendid specimen of Dutch art, and friends of mine who are art critics have praised very much the work of Chall-ener, which has recently been added to the gallery. We have lately increased the amount to be devoted to this work, and we have provided that these works are to be purchased under the advice of a committee of artists to be chosen from the members of the Royal Canadian Academy. I have no doubt that by this means there will be added to the gallery in the future, works of merit.' I trust that before long we will have a building worthy of Canadian art, and that there will be a national museum in this capital city, which will include a picture gallery in which will be exhibited the finest works of our country. I would not, however, like to have these confined entirely to the works of Canadian artists, because 1 feel that we should have accessible there, for the inspiration and study of Canadian artists, paintings, by the masters of the old country. I must confess that I would advise the purchase of first-class works of foreign schools. We are young in art but we are making progress. As an encouragement to my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) I would say that I have made arrangements with the Royal Canadian Academy to assist them out of the funds which parliament has voted, to secure a representative and creditable exhibition of Canadian art at St. Louis exhibition. At the Pan-American exhibition the Canadian academy made a most creditable showing, and I believe that at the greater exhibition which is to be held in St. Louis, Canadian artists will be able to achieve even greater success than at Buffalo. I again thank my hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) for the patriotic words he has uttered

on behalf of Canadian art, and I trust they will sink into the minds of all who hear them and of all who will read them.

In mentioning a few names of Canadian artists, I might have included Cote, and Forbes, and Knowles, and Sherwood, and others of great ability. As to the suggestion of the hon. minister that the selection of paintings should be left entirely to artists, I must say that is an open question. There are no more jealous men in the world than artists, they all admit it themselves. We have in the history of English art the name of the celebrated portrait painter Romney, one of the grandest that British art has ever produced; and yet he had to struggle on and be kept out of recognition from the very first, by the jealousy of men like Sir Joshua Reynolds, though he was far superior to them all. Therefore we should not lose sight of the fact that artists as a class are very jealous of each other, and good art critics who have the means of possessing themselves of specimens of art should have some recognition.
Mr. IiACKETT. I am very much pleased indeed to find that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is endeavouring to encourage art in this country. I desire to state in this connection that one of the gentlemen he has named, Mr. Harris, of Montreal, is a native of Prince Edward Island. In the encouragement of art and learning, our small province has not been neglected. Grant to assist the Canadian Association for the prevention of tuberculosis, $2,000.
What is that for ? Is that in connection with cattle ?

No, it is in connection with the association which was formed in Ottawa two or three years ago under the patronage of His Excellency, following the lead of the association which was formed in Great Britain under the patronage of His Majesty the King, for the purpose of spreading information amongst the people at large as to how the spread of the dread disease of tuberculosis could be prevented and lessened by ordinary means independent of medical practice. I have here a memorandum from the secretary of the association, in which he states that a large amount of literature is being sent out. The secretary himself is devoting his whole time to the work. He goes about the country at the request of medical associations and gives lectures and explanations with regard to it. The association holds an annual meeting in Ottawa, at which papers
are read by eminent medical gentlemen, and these are printed and distributed throughout the country. The money is used chiefly in paying the secretary and in defraying the cost of distributing the literature.

I was at the annual meeting of the association, which I think will be productive of good ; but it occurred to me that additional benefit might result if articles were written and sent periodically for publication in local papers, giving directions regarding the prevention of the disease. It must take more than this amount of money to keep the association up.

There is a subscription for membership in the association. I dot not think any fee is exacted, but a large number of people have subscribed various sums, some of them quite handsome sums, towards its expenses.

Extensive repairs are now being made to the engines and boilers by Bruce Stewart & Company, Charlottetown, by day's labour. The boilers are fourteen years old, and, owing to the severe test these parts are exposed to and the nature of the work, the boilers and1 machinery require to be kept in the best condition possible. Besides the repairs to the engines and boilers the deck-houses became loose and are being thoroughly and strongly repaired. These repairs will be the means of putting the ship in excellent condition for thei winter ice work. The department considers that the repairs to the 'Stanley' to make her fit for the winter work will not exceed $15,000. If the ship had been sent to England to her builders to be repaired, the cost wiould be in the vicinity of $40,000, if! not more, as the expenses of the taking the vessel to England and keeping a crew would be considerable.	,

Iu addition to the repairs to the ' Stanley ' and the ' Lansdowne,' I may say that when the ' Minto ' and the ' Stanley ' were icebound last winter, there was a possibility of both steamers being pushed ashore by the ice, and, in that event these valuable ships would certainly have been lost.

speechtext: It is very important to tile island that communication should be maintained winter and summer between it and the mainland. speechtext:
I presume that the hon. gentleman desires to do what is right, and I hope therefore he will see his way clear to placing the * Stanley ' on the route between Summerside and Cape Tormentine. There is another question of great importance and that is the building of a third boat for the island. We have during the session voted away millions of dollars to other provinces, and I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that there is no province in this Dominion more deserving of consideration than the province of Prince Edward Island. I insist that the third boat shall be constructed for the purpose of maintaining that com-

munication. Yesterday we had a question on the Order paper by my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) with regard to the loss sustained by the shippers of frozen fish and other products from that province.
I would like to have the minister tell us if he intends to compensate these people for the loss sustained.
The question was put yesterday, and I answered that the claims had been received and that the matter was under consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is a very plausible answer, but I insist on having something more definite. Is it the intention of the government to compensate the young men of Prince Edward Island for the losses they sustained?

Every legitimate claim, of course, will be entertained. But all have to be looked into, and the Department of Justice lias to be consulted as to whether we are responsible or not. It is a very serious question, as the hon. gentleman knows, and we have to take the necessary precautions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister is very cautious. He wants to be advised by the Minister of Justice. I insist that this is a case for the consideration of the government. We have no legal claim against them at all. But the loss arose through the failure of the government boat to carry the freight from Georgetown to Pictou. Will not the minister himself, as having charge of these boats and knowing the circumstances through which the loss arose, grant the young men of Prince Edward Island compensation for the loss which they have sustained ?

I shall certainly not come to a decision without consulting the Department of Justice, for our decision involves immediately a very large amount. Then there is the question of law to be decided, for it may be that this case would establish a precedent. Under the circumstances, my hon. friend (Mr. ITackett) must see that the question cannot be decided offhand. It may be necessary to appoint experts to ascertain the amounts, and also whether the interruption to navigation was inevitable, or whether it was caused by the officers of the department. These things have to be looked into, but the hon. gentleman knows very well that we have been (busy with the session of parliament ever since the claims have been presented, so that, whatever my desire to do justice to these people, there has been no opportunity to adjust the claims.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I allege no legal claim against any officer of the department or
against the minister. But I would like to have the minister consider the fact that the young men of Prince Edward Island had their products ready for the market, and those products were delayed at Georgetown on account of the absence of the government steamer. This is not a legal case. Our young men are not going to go to law with the government. What we insist upon is that the government, in their own way, shall grant to the people of Prince Edward Island compensation for the losses sustained.

This matter is of the utmost importance to the people of Prince Edward Island. Early in the session 1 reviewed the history of the boats engaged in the work of maintaining communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland last winter. We certainly do not want a recurrence of the disastrous events of that season, events due, as I pointed out, to neglect on the part of the department and bad administration at the island end of the winter boat service. The minister, on that occasion, said that he intended to take a trip to the island to look into the question of placing the boats so as to prevent a recurrence of what took place last winter. As we all know, the session has kept the minister here, and he will not have time to go to the island this year. The session is likely to go on for tour or five weeks yet, and, by that time, the 'Stanley' and 'Minto' should be placed and shippers should know exactly where the boats are going to ply. Last year, after the ' Northumberland,' the summer boat, stopped at Summerside, it was over a fortnight before the ' Stanley ' was put on the route between Summerside and Cape Tormentine, and even then it was after much telegraphing and humbugging between the department here and the agent of the department at Prince Edward Island. Anybody who looks over the correspondence of that time will be appalled at the humbugging that went on before that boat was put upon the route from Cape Tormentine to Summer-side. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that that is not a desirable state of affairs; and, while he will not be able to visit Prince Edward Island to look into the facts himself, he knows that shippers to and from the island need to be informed in good time as to the arrangements to be made. There are goods coming through from the United Kingdom, from the United States and from the upper provinces, and shippers must know how they are to send their goods. They want to know whether the 1 Stanley ' will be on the route between Summerside and Cape Tormentine immediately after the summer boat is withdrawn. That is the vital point. The matter should not be delayed until the summer boats stop, and then have a repetition of the humbugging that went on last year, when shippers could not get freight rates and could not learn where the boats would ply. And

even when we did get the * Stanley,' she was in Georgetown cutting boats out of the ice instead of rendering the service she should have rendered at the beginning of the winter. This is- a most vital question to the commercial interests of Prince Edward Island. The neglect of last year in carrying out the compact by not arranging for these boats in good time, and using the ' Minto ' to cut the ' Stanley ' free when she was caught in the ice at Summerside-these things are responsible for the condition of affairs from which we suffered last winter. My hon. friend from West Prince (Mr. Hackett) has called attention to the way in which the shippers suffered loss because the ' Minto ' was taken off her legitimate course and taken to the relief of the ' Stanley,' which had been caught in the ice, where she remained for two months and had finally to be taken out by the government of Prince Edward Island, assisted by the board of trade. I pointed out the legal aspect of the question when I brought it before the House. If the question is to be decided on the legal merits of the claim, there are strong facts bearing on the case to be considered. But, as the hon. member for West Prince said, we do not want to compel these men to take legal action against the government. It is the duty of the government, under the circumstances, to consider more than the legal aspects of the case. The goods were waiting at Georgetown to be transported across to Pictou, and they were not transported because the government, whose duty it was to provide the means of transportation, had failed to do so. It is the duty of the government to compensate the people for the loss they sustained on that occasion. Before I sit down I would like to have an assurance from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that this matter will not be left until the last moment, and that the people of Prince Edward Island will be notified that the boat ' Stanley ' will be put on the route from Summerside to Cape Tormentine, at least as long as there is open navigation to those points, and that the ' Minto ' will be placed on the Charlottetown and Georgetown to Pictou route.

I am very anxious indeed to see our mercantile marine a sue-

cess, and I think the Minister of Marine has the same object in view as myself. In order to accomplish what we both desire, it is necessary that our young men who desire to follow the sea for a livelihood should be given every opportunity to prepare themselves for their calling by a suitable education. It would be therefore, advisable to open marine schools in some of the most important ports in the maritime provinces. And I would ask for one in my own town, which represents an amount of shipping beyond that of any other county. There are more vessels belonging to Lunenburg, I believe, than to all the other counties combined. I would suggest that a school be opened in that place in order that we should be able to advance our young men as far as possible in preparation for their work in connection with navigation. I am sure that the effect will be to advance the interests of the whole country.

There is another item in the supplementary estimates providing for the special study of schools of navigation. At present I am only following what has been done by my predecessors and voting enough money to maintain existing services. pect a salary, because be accepted the appoint meut with the understanding that he should only receive the fees. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that instead of increasing the examinations there might very well be less, by concentrating them in a few places. You have two examiners in some places and in other places only one. Now, is a certificate granted by one examiner just as good as a certificate granted by three ? There should be some system. I really think this whole department requires a very severe shaking up. There is no reason why at Sydney, for instance, a man should go before one examiner and be granted a certificate, whereas at another place he requires to go before three examiners to get a certificate. The thing is absurd on the face of it. Instead of having examiners at a number of little places like Sydney, you should have a board of examiners at the great ports of the country.

speechtext: Is there anything for this life-saving station on the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with reference to which the Prime Minister told us to-day the government would make a harbour of refuge, and where a life-saving station was needed ?
Not yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would the minister give us the names of the life saving stations in Ontario ?
On the great Lakes, Cobourg, Collingwood, Goderich, Pelee Island, Poplar-Point, Port Hope, Port Colborne, Port Rowan, Port Stanley, Toronto, Wellington, Consecon, Long Point (Lake Erie) Kincardine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I wish to draw the minister's attention to a very important place on Lake Ontario, in the county which I have the honour to represent-Port Credit. There is a volunteer crew there at the present time, which has been organized for several years. It has rescued several vessels that have been driven out on their way to the city of Toronto. I think it is a place which should be made a permanent station.
I will call the attention of my officers to it, and have a report made upon it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the minister do that soon ?	-
As soon ns possible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
If the department make the examination and And what services have been rendered by this volunteer crew, I think they will feel it to be their duty to establish a service at that point.
Further amount required for investigation into wrecks, $2,000.

This is on the recommendation of Captain Salmon. This board is completely organized under him at the present time. Of course, it does not entail as much work as the organization of the examiners. But it was found that the amount of $2,000 was not sufficient to hold the examination asked for by the insurance companies and the British Board of Trade. We have adopted the rule in the department of holding an investigation into every casualty to ascertain who is responsible, whether it is the channel, the men in charge of the boats, or the boats. The results of all these investigations have been transmitted to the British Board of Trade.
Mr. FOWIjER. How many were there last year ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Fifteen. This year, I think, we have already held twelve.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:

The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Last	year we had not enough
money. We spent $4,000.

If I understand it correctly, Mr. Salmon is practically a commissioner to make all these inquiries.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. He is a commissioner of investigation under the law, and he has associated with him two expert assessors.
Do the same men do the work all through ?

No. Two assessors are taken from each place where he holds an investigation.
For expenses of inquiry into the subject of a Naval Militia and School of Navigation, $7,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is this something new- a naval-militia ?

There was originally asked $5,000, and the amount has been increased by $2,500 in order to enable us to study the system of establishing this naval reserve, of which so much has been said. It may be necessary to send an officer to some other countries in order to see howr the same thing is organized in these countries. It may be necessary to send this officer to some other country to see how that is organized elsewhere. The school of navigation established last winter in Montreal gave very good satisfaction and I shall have a copy of the report made and put before the House. It is very interesting and shows that Captain Salmon knows the subject very well. These schools should be encouraged and the amount of $5,000 should not be considered too much. '	-
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is the number of the staff ?

In Montreal they had four professors and the school was attended by about fifty pupils. There were lectures given on thirty-two subjects.
Gratuity to Alfred Couillard second mate of steamer ' Druid ' for injuries while on duty, $600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This poor fellow lost an eye while on duty. He claimed $1,000, and consented to accept $600.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I wish to commend the action of the hon. minister in granting this gratuity to this officer and I desire to take this opportunity to point out the different treatment accorded to officials on the Intercolonial when any accident occurs to them. Last year an accident took place near Belmont on the line of the Intercolonial. Several persons were killed in the accident and one brakesman severely injured. It was a miracle he was not killed. He had several ribs and a leg broken. He was laid up and unable to work some six or eight months. During that time all that he received was three dollars a week, which he got as a member of an insurance association. To show how differently he was treated from this man, let me point to this fact. His run was to Moncton, and as he was unable to get into Moncton on account of the wreck, he was only paid half a day for that day. That sort of treatment cannot be too severely condemned. It is not the treatment which would be accorded by any private firm or corporation to its employees. There is not a man in business who would use an employee in that way, when that employee was injured in his service, without any fault on the employee's part. This man was injured in the service of the Intercolonial, and they would not pay him his full day's wage on ihe day of his accident because he was unable to reach Moncton where his day's run ended. I am glad to sec that the Department of Marine and Fisheries treats its employees in a different manner. I would ask the hon. minister to look into this case- the case of Brakeman Crandall-who was injured in the Belmont disaster. He has a wife and large family, and all he got was $3 per week from an insurance company.

I have not had that particular case before me, but I promise to look into it. I would remind my hon. friend that this insurance fund to which he refers is supported to a considerable extent by the government and that fact may have been taken into consideration. However, I do not offer an opinion as to whether the compensation was adequate and will inquire into the matter.

I would like to suggest that if the hon. gentleman who is leading the House would consult with the right lion, the Prime Minister as to what items on the paper shall be dropped and what gone on with, we could estimate better how long we are likely to be kept here.

My right hon. friend the Prime Minister will make such a statement probably to-morrow, certainly not later than Monday. The Bill which the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has in charge, and which is being transferred to government Orders, with respect to the election law, will be taken up to-morrow.
